And I name them for this reason wineskins, and I say that the base man is filled "with wine of the vine of Sodom," is filled with Egyptian wine and with the wine of the enemies of Israel, whereas the holy man who has been benefited is filled with wine from the vine Sorek and with the wine concerning which it is written: "Your cup that inebriates, how excellent it is," and again the holy man is filled with wine from that which Wisdom mixed. Let these things, then, be understood by me according to vice and virtue, so that the "every wineskin is filled with wine" may be contemplated. But if we must also see the things that come through vice and through virtue — punishments through vice, but blessings and promises through virtue — let us demonstrate from the sacred writings in what manner the punishments and the promises are called wine: "Take the cup of this unmixed wine, and you shall give all the nations to drink, to whom I shall send you." Jeremiah says these things; to which he adds: "And they shall drink and vomit and go mad and fall." So then he named the punishments here unmixed wine, which those drink who are worthy of unmixed wine, that is, of unmixed punishment. But there are also others who drink a punishment that is not unmixed, but mingled; for "a cup in the Lord's hand, full of unmixed wine of mingling, he inclined from this to that; yet its dregs were not emptied out; all the sinners of the earth shall drink." And if you wish also to see a cup of blessing, which the righteous drink, that of Wisdom would indeed have sufficed, in which she said: "Drink wine which I have mingled for you"; but behold for me also the Savior going up for the Passover into "a large upper room, furnished and adorned," and keeping the feast with his disciples and giving them a cup, concerning which it is written not that he mingled it; for Jesus, gladdening his disciples, gladdens them with unmixed wine, and says to them: "Take, drink, this is my blood, which is poured out for you for the forgiveness of sins; do this, as often as you drink it, in remembrance of me," and: "Amen I say to you, I shall not drink it from now on, until I drink it new with you in the kingdom of God."

Do you see the promise, which is "the cup of the new covenant"? Do you see the punishments as a cup of unmixed wine, and another kind of punishment as a mingled cup — so that it is mixed for each according to the worth of good action mingled with wretched action, which they will drink? Understand for me, on the one hand, those who are wholly alien to piety toward God and give no heed to themselves at all, but live at random, as drinking the unmixed wine concerning which we set forth the words from Jeremiah; but on the other hand, those who have not wholly fallen away, and yet are sinners — but unworthy of the cup "of the new covenant," doing at one time more upright, at another time contrary actions — as drinking wine "of unmixed mingling." For God "inclined from this to that." Of what "this"? I behold two cups, according to what is said: "He inclined from this to that; yet its dregs were not emptied out." Understand for me the cup of your good works in the one hand of God; but if you wish me to speak more boldly, let there be in the right hand of God the cup of your good works, and then let there be your cup of sins in the left hand of God. So then, when you are about to be punished for your sins — since more upright works too have come from you — "there is in the Lord's hand a cup of unmixed wine, full of mingling. And he inclined from this to that," from that in the left hand to that in the right. For neither can you drink only the cup of good things, as one who has not done only good works, nor can you drink only the cup of sins, for some upright things have been done by you. For this reason "he inclined from this to that." According to the proportion of your works, the wrath and the punishment are mixed for you, so that the punishment may be either more watery for you or sharper and more painful. For according to the proportion, as I said before, of the sins compared with the good deeds, that which is given from the cup of wrath is somehow blunted or is not blunted, a certain amount being given for each of the sins. But if you are wholly good and virtuous, you say: "I will take the cup of salvation, and I will call upon the name of the Lord." "Every wineskin," then, whether good or wretched, "shall be filled with wine," and according to the fitness of the wineskin wine shall be cast into the wineskin, according to the account of the wineskins named here. Oil, then, is not put into the wineskins, nor any other liquid matter, but every wineskin must be filled with wine.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then he teaches, on account of those who had sinned — as far as the literal sense goes — in Jerusalem at that time and in Judea, with what sort of wine God is about to fill these wineskins, the sinners. For it is written: "If they say to you: Do we not surely know that every wineskin shall be filled with wine? then you shall say to them: Thus says the Lord: Behold, I fill all the inhabitants of this land, and the kings who sit as sons of David upon his throne, and the priests." He who is about to punish spares no one. Not because someone bore the title of prophet, yet has sins, will he not be filled with the threats that are spoken. Not because someone bore the title of priest and seemed to hold the preeminence of a more honorable name among the people does God spare him, so that he should not be punished when he has sinned. But the things recorded concerning those people, the apostle says, were written for our sake, "upon whom the ends of the ages have come." If, then, anyone even among these priests (and I point to us, the presbyters), or among these Levites who surround the people (I mean the deacons), sins, he will have this punishment; just as, again, there are certain priestly blessings, concerning which, God granting it, not far off but after the examination of the prophetic word, we shall learn when Numbers is read; for concerning priests certain things are about to be said there.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And the priests," then, "and the prophets and Judah and all the inhabitants of Jerusalem" God says he will fill "with drunkenness" and will scatter "them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons." And let us understand these things also thus: the righteous God gathers together, but the sinners he scatters. For this reason, at the time when men did not move from the east, God did not scatter them; but when they moved "from the east" and "a man said to his neighbor: Come, and let us build for ourselves a city and a tower, whose top shall be up to heaven," God says concerning these: "Come, and going down let us confound their language there," and each one is confounded and is scattered to some place of the earth. And the people of Israel too, so long as they did not sin, were in Judea, but when they sinned they are scattered thereafter from the inhabited world and dispersed everywhere.

Understand something of this sort for me concerning all of us as well. There is a certain church of the firstborn who are enrolled in the heavens, where is Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem. The blessed will be gathered together there, so that they may be together. But in this very thing the sinners are punished, in not being with one another. I know of some in this life who, for the sake of punishment, wish to hand over to some island, and for the sake of torment scatter the household of one who has offended the kingdom — the wife here, one son here, then the other elsewhere — so that not even in their misfortune may the mother enjoy the company of the son, or the brother of the brother. Understand something of this sort also in the case of the unjust. It is necessary that you, the sinner, taste something more bitter, being managed by God, so that being disciplined you may be saved. And just as you punish the household servant or son who is punished by you, not simply wishing to torture him, but that you may turn him back by the sufferings, so also God will discipline with the sufferings that come from afflictions those who do not turn back at the word, who have not been healed. He casts about, for the sake of discipline, the things he casts about, according to what is said: "Continually with suffering and scourge you shall be disciplined, Jerusalem." So then, in order that the disciplining suffering may increase, those who suffer are scattered from one another, so that this one and that one may not be together. For the intensity of the suffering would be relaxed through the consolation of each one toward the other.

But if we must add to the discussion yet another cause of the scattering, this too I shall set forth. Wicked men, being together with one another, contemplate evils and increase them, just as good men, being together with the good, deliberate about good things. [And] therefore the evil counsel is dissolved and divided — which would have prevailed with those like it — when the wretched are scattered from one another. For this reason God arranges that the base should not be with one another, perhaps even taking forethought for them, so that their wickedness may not grow together, but may be diminished by being dissolved. These things because of the "I will scatter them, a man and his brother, and their fathers and their sons together. Says the Lord."

"I will not long for them, and I will not spare, and I will not have pity, from their destruction."

Those from the heresies pounce upon such literal statements, saying: Do you see what sort the Demiurge is? The God of the prophets, who says: "I will not spare and I will not have pity, from their destruction"? How can this one be good? But if I take as an example the judge who, for the sake of the common good, does not have pity, and the magistrate who rightly does not show mercy, I shall be able from the example to persuade that God, in sparing many, does not spare one. And I shall take as an example also a physician, showing that in sparing the whole body he does not spare one member. For instance, let this be set before a judge: to fashion peace and to prepare what is advantageous for the nation under him. And let there come forward some murderer brought to trial, fair in appearance and beautiful to behold. Let a mother come forward, offering pitiful words to the judge, so that her old age may be pitied; let the wife of this man who is unworthy to be pitied plead; let children standing around him beg on his behalf. In these circumstances, what is advantageous for the community? Is it that this man be pitied, or that he not be pitied? But if he is pitied, he will return to the same deeds; whereas if he is not pitied, he himself will die, but the community will be improved. So too God, if he spares the sinner and pities him and has compassion so as not to punish him — who will not be made worse? Which of the base, who cease from their sins even because of the fears of the places of punishment, will not be made worse, will not become worse? Such things can be seen happening in the churches too. Someone sinned, and after the sin he asked for communion. If he is too quickly pitied, the community is worn down. The sin of others grows. But if, by reasoning — not as one unmerciful nor as one savage is the judge, but as one taking forethought even for the one, and yet taking more forethought for the many than for the one — he considers the harm that will come to the community from the communion of the one and from the pardon of his sin, it is clear that he will cause the one to be cast out, so that he may save the many.

Behold for me also a physician, in what manner, if he is sparing about cutting what must be cut, if he is sparing about cauterizing what must be cauterized because of the pains that follow upon such remedies, in what manner the disease increases and becomes worse. But if he approaches the cutting and the burning somewhat more boldly, he will heal by not pitying, by seeming not to have compassion on the one who is cauterized and the one who is cut. So too God does not manage one man only, but manages the whole world, and administers everywhere the things in heaven and the things on earth. He considers, then, what is advantageous for the whole world and for all beings, and, as far as possible, he considers also what is advantageous for the one — yet not so that the advantage of the one should come to the detriment of the world. For this reason eternal fire too has been prepared, for this reason gehenna also has been made ready, for this reason there is also a certain outer darkness, of which there is need not only because of the one being punished, but especially because of the community.

But if you wish to take Scripture as a witness that sinners are punished even for the instruction of others, even if these are at some time despaired of as regards healing, hear Solomon saying in the Proverbs: "When a pestilent man is scourged, the fool will become more shrewd." He did not say that the one being scourged himself will become more shrewd and more prudent because of the scourges, but he says that the fool is changed from folly to prudence because of the scourges applied to the pestilent man; for this is what is signified here by the name of "shrewdness." And the fool is changed through seeing others being scourged. So then the punishment of others is advantageous to us, if indeed we become worthy of salvation through others being punished. And as the transgression of Israel was of profit to the salvation of the nations, so the punishment of some will be of profit to the salvation of others. For this reason, being good, God says: "I will not spare and I will not have pity, from their destruction."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Now that the one section has been circumscribed, let us see also what the other teaches us: "Hear and give ear, and be not lifted up, for the Lord has spoken. Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, and before your feet stumble upon dark mountains; and you will wait for light, and there will be a shadow of death there, and they will be set in darkness. But if you do not hear secretly, your soul will weep before the face of insolence, and your eyes will bring down tears, because the flock of the Lord has been crushed." He wishes these same people to hear and to give ear, being satisfied neither with their merely hearing nor with their merely giving ear. Therefore he says: "Hear and give ear." Then, after this, he commands them not to be lifted up, and teaches what must be done. What, then, is "to hear" and what is "to give ear," let us consider from the very wording. The "give ear" is "receive into the ears," and the "hear," if it is said in contradistinction to the "give ear," perhaps is "receive into the understanding." And among the things said in the Scriptures, some are more secret and more mystical, but others are useful straightaway to those who understand. Concerning the more secret things, I think, the "hear" is said, but concerning the things that are useful straightaway and able to benefit the hearer without interpretation, the "give ear"; if, then, we examine the whole of Scripture, we shall say, "having become approved money-changers": this, on the one hand, hear; this, on the other hand, give ear to.

Then, when we have heard and given ear, he commands us: "And be not lifted up." For "everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled." And the Savior too, in saying: "Learn from me, that I am gentle and lowly in heart, and you shall find rest for your souls," teaches us not to be lifted up. For along with the other human evils, this sin too is much in us — at one time when we are lifted up quite unreasonably, and over that for which one ought not to be lifted up even to any degree, but at another time with plausibility, because that over which we are lifted up is reasonable, and yet the being lifted up even over that is not sound.

What I mean will be clear thus: there are some who are lifted up because they are sons of governors and because they are of a family among those of great worldly dignities. Such men, being lifted up over a matter that lies outside their choice and is indifferent, do not have even a reasonable plausibility that is brought forward to lead them toward being lifted up. There are those who are lifted up because they have authority to put men to death, and lifted up because they have received among themselves the advancement, so called, of such a kind as to cut off the heads of men. "The glory" of such men "is in their shame." Others are lifted up over wealth — not the true wealth but the lower — and others are lifted up, for example, over having a fine house or many fields. None of these things is worthy of account; one ought not to be lifted up over any of these.

But the plausible occasion for being lifted up is when someone is lifted up because he is wise, and is lifted up conscious to himself that already from the age of ten he has not touched sexual pleasures, or even from boyhood has not touched them; and again another is lifted up because he has worn bonds for Christ's sake. There is here a plausibility suggesting that one is reasonably lifted up; yet not even over these things, as regards the true reckoning, is one reasonably lifted up. Thus it is not reasonable to be lifted up even over these things. Paul had the material for being lifted up on account of the visions, on account of the sights, on account of the wonders and signs, on account of the labors which he labored for Christ, on account of the churches which he founded, being ambitious, where Christ had not been named, to lay the foundation of a church. All these were material for him — if one must speak with the plausibility concerning being lifted up — so that it might have seemed to some that he was rightly lifted up. But nevertheless, since not even the being lifted up over such things is without danger, the good Father, as he had granted him visions and sights, so also gave him, in the portion of a gift of grace, "an angel of Satan, to buffet him, so that he should not be over-exalted." And concerning this he besought the Lord three times, that "the angel of Satan," who had been given to him precisely so that he should not be lifted up, might depart from him. And the Lord answered him (for Paul was worthy of an answer from the Lord) and said to him: "My grace is sufficient for you; for my power is perfected in weakness." Over nothing, then, ought one to be lifted up; for falling follows upon being lifted up, according to the "before crushing the heart of a man is exalted, and before glory it is humbled." Let these things suffice for the "Hear and give ear, and be not lifted up, for the Lord has spoken."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
And let us see also what he bids us do after these things: "Give," he says, "to the Lord our God glory before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon dark mountains; and you will wait for light." He wishes the one who gives "glory to God" to give "glory to God" while there is light, since the glory of God cannot be proclaimed once it has grown dark and darkness has come. When, then, does it grow dark, and when does the darkening not occur? "Work while the light is in you." "The light is in" you if you have in you the one who said: "I am the light of the world." As long as this rises for you, glorify God; but know that a certain darkening can occur, and one must not let this darkening remain, but must give glory to God before it grows dark.

Perhaps we shall understand what is written by using an evangelical saying spoken by the Savior which runs thus: "Work while it is day; night comes when no one is able to work." He named there this present age "day" (but I necessarily added the "there"; for I know that in other places other things again are indicated) — he named, then, this present age "day," but darkness and night the consummation, because of the punishments. For "why do you desire the day of the Lord? And this is darkness and not light," says the prophet Amos. If you see what the gloom is after the consummation of the world, that which follows when almost the whole race of men is punished for the things they have sinned, you will see that then that which surrounds has grown dark, and no one any longer is able to glorify God, seeing that the word of God commanded even the righteous, saying: "Go, my people, enter into your chamber, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while, until the wrath of my anger pass by." And at the same time, in these words, let anyone who is able observe that he said: "a little while." But that "little while" is little for God; it is not little for a man; for one must see that for each thing there is something little and something great. And from an example I shall demonstrate that for each thing there is something little or great. For every animal such-and-such an amount of food is little in comparison with its constitution, and such-and-such an amount of food is much again in comparison with its constitution. And thus what is little for a man is great for another animal. What is little, for example, for a man is much for a child. Thus the whole time of human life is little, even the time of the long-lived man, in comparison with the whole of the entire present age. So indeed the "little" of God is much in comparison with us, and a whole age is the "little" of God. If, then, it is said: "Go, my people, enter into your chambers, shut your door, hide yourself for a little while," that "little" must be thought to be spoken not in relation to the condition of the one commanded to go and to enter into his chambers, but in relation to the condition of the one who commands these things, for whom that which is much for this man is little. For if, "until the wrath of the anger" of God "pass by," some must enter into their chambers, and there are those for whom "the sins are not forgiven, not only throughout this whole age but also throughout the whole age to come," it is clear that the "little" is extended alongside the things that have been said.

"Give," therefore, "glory to the Lord our God." How do we give glory to the Lord our God? It is not in voices and little phrases that I seek the giving of glory to the Lord our God, but in deeds the one who gives glory to the Lord God gives glory to him. Glorify God in self-control (sōphrosynē), in righteousness, in doing good glorify God; give glory to God in courage and endurance, give glory to God in piety and holiness and the remaining virtues. And if these things are so, and one glorifies God in this way, then if I state the opposite, do not think that I am blaspheming; for I will bring forward the Scripture as a witness of those things too. The self-controlled man glorifies God, the one who lives licentiously dishonors God. For, like Nebuchadnezzar, he overturns the temple of God and "corrupts the temple of God" and "through the transgression of the law dishonors God" (this too is an apostolic expression). The sinner, then, clothes God with dishonor. And questions are raised concerning providence, so that some doubt whether providence exists; but providence is nothing other than [what is questioned] on account of evil. Take away the evil, and you do not stumble against providence. But up and down those who stumble against providence say these things: why are there so many adulterers and so many effeminate men, why are there so many godless and impious people? And it is the sinners who beget dishonor for providence, stumbling-blocks against God, blasphemy against the one who created the world. Some, then, do give glory to God, but they do not give glory to God who do the things opposite to the glory of God through their sins.

"Give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon the dark mountains." There are certain dark mountains, there are certain luminous mountains; but since there are both. The luminous mountains are the holy angels of God, the prophets, Moses the servant, the apostles of Jesus Christ. All these are luminous mountains, and I think it is concerning these that it has been said in the Psalms: "His foundations are in the holy mountains." But what sort of mountains are dark? Those who raise up high things against the knowledge of God. The devil is a dark mountain; the rulers of this age who are being brought to nothing are dark mountains; and the demon, the epilepsy (moon-affliction), was a mountain, and it was a dark mountain, concerning which the Savior said: "You shall say to this mountain." For when the discussion concerned the epilepsy and the disciples said, "Why were we not able to cast it out?", the Savior answers that "if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you shall say to this mountain," concerning which you put forward the question, concerning which you inquired, "you shall say to this mountain: Move from here to there, and it shall move." "From here" — away from the man; "there" — to its own proper place. Those, then, who stumble do not stumble upon luminous mountains, but upon dark mountains, whenever they come to be with the devil and his angels, the dark mountains.

"And you shall wait for light." Now "and you shall wait for light" can be joined to "give glory to the Lord our God." If you give glory to the Lord our God before it grows dark, before your feet stumble upon dark mountains," it is clear that, even if it does grow dark, "you shall wait for the light" and the light shall receive you in succession. But another might say (I do not know whether he is thinking soundly or not) that even those who stumble "upon dark mountains" shall wait beside the dark mountains, waiting for the light of mercy; for this is what "and you shall wait for light" would seem to mean. But when one comes upon the dark mountains, let us see what is there: "the shadow of death." Where the dark mountains are, there is the shadow of death, begotten from those very dark mountains; "and they shall be set in darkness."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." Of those who hear, some hear in secret, but others, even if they hear, do not hear in secret. What then is it to hear in secret, other than "but we speak the wisdom of God in a mystery, the hidden wisdom, which God foreordained before the ages for our glory"? And again elsewhere it is said that "the greater part of the works of God are in hidden things." If I hear the law, either I hear in secret or I do not hear in secret. The Jew does not hear the law in secret; therefore he is circumcised openly, not knowing that "the Jew is not the one in the open, nor is circumcision that which is in the open in the flesh." But he who hears about circumcision in secret shall be circumcised in what is hidden; he who hears in secret the things enacted by law concerning the Passover eats of the lamb Christ (for "Christ our Passover has been sacrificed"), and knowing what sort of thing the flesh of the Word is, and knowing that "it is true food," he partakes of it; for he heard about the Passover in secret. But this great mass of the Jew, for this reason, killed the Lord Jesus and is even today guilty of the murder of Jesus, since he heard neither the law nor the prophets in secret. If you read about the unleavened bread, it is possible to hear in secret, it is possible to hear the commandment openly. As many of you (for the Passover is near) as keep the unleavened bread, the bodily unleavened bread, do not hear the commandment that says: "If you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep." And concerning the Sabbath, women who have not heard the prophet do not hear in secret, but hear openly. They do not wash on the day of the Sabbath, they return "to the poor and weak elements," as though Christ had not sojourned among us, the one who perfects us and carries us over from the elements of the law to the perfection of the Gospel.

Therefore let us take heed as we read the law and the prophets, lest we ever fall under the prophecy that says: "But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." As many of you as observe the Jewish fast, as though not understanding the day of atonement, keep it after the sojourn of Jesus Christ. You did not hear about the atonement in secret, but you heard openly; for to hear about the atonement in secret is to hear how God made Jesus a propitiation concerning our sins, and that "he is the propitiation concerning our sins, and not concerning ours only, but also concerning the whole world." And even if evangelical parables are read and the hearer is of those outside, he will not hear them in secret. But if the hearer is an apostle or one of those who enter "into the house" of Jesus, he approaches Jesus, and he inquires also about the obscurity of the parable, and Jesus interprets it, and that hearer of the Gospel comes to hear it in secret, so that his soul may not weep; for the soul of those who do not hear in secret weeps.

Why, marvelously, did he not say: you shall weep, if you do not hear in secret, but rather: "your soul shall weep"? There is a certain weeping of the soul alone weeping, and perhaps the Savior teaches us that weeping when he says: "There shall be the weeping." And even if he says: "Woe to you who laugh now, for you shall mourn and weep," he speaks concerning that weeping, which the prophet here also threatens, saying: "But if you do not hear in secret, your soul shall weep before the face of insolence." For when you are treated with insolence, then you shall weep and your eyes shall bring down tears, "because the flock of the Lord has been crushed." If someone now looks at the affairs of the Jews and compares them with the ancient things, he will see in what manner "the flock of the Lord has been crushed." For this was once the flock of the Lord, and since they judged themselves unworthy, the word was turned to the nations. If, then, that flock of the Lord was crushed, ought not we, the wild olive, grafted contrary to its own nature into the cultivated olive of the fathers, to fear all the more, lest this "flock of the Lord" too be crushed? For it is destined to be crushed at some time, according to what was said by the Savior, when "because lawlessness is multiplied, the love of the many shall grow cold." For concerning whom is the word? Is not "the love of the many shall grow cold" said concerning those called Christians? Concerning whom is the word, that "yet when the Son of Man comes, will he then find faith upon the earth"? Is it not concerning us? Therefore let us take heed to ourselves in all that we do, so that day by day this flock of God may be made better, may be made healthy, may be healed, and that all crushing may depart from our souls, so that we may be perfected in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: It will serve us to remember that what is called the Word came to certain persons, as "the word of the Lord which came to Hosea, the son of Beeri," and "the word which came to Isaiah, the son of Amoz, concerning Judah and concerning Jerusalem," and "the word that came to Jeremiah concerning the drought." We must inquire how this Word came to Hosea, and how it came also to Isaiah the son of Amoz, and again to Jeremiah concerning the drought. The comparison may enable us to find out how the Word was with God. We will generalize by simply looking at what the prophets said, as if that were the Word of the Lord or the Word that came to them. May it not be … that … the Son, the Word, of whom we are now theologizing, came to Hosea, sent to him by the Father, historically, that is to say, to the son of Beeri, the prophet Hosea.… Similarly the Word comes also to Isaiah, teaching the things that are coming on Judea and Jerusalem in the last days. So also it comes to Jeremiah lifted up by a divine elation.… Thus to find out what is meant by the phrase "the Word was with God," we have adduced the words used about the prophets, how he came to Hosea, to Isaiah, to Jeremiah.… We have to add that in his coming to the prophets he illuminates the prophets with the light of knowledge, causing them to see things that had been before them but that they had not understood until then.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 2:1

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What a state the person is in who has deserted the easy yoke and the light burden of Christ to subject himself once again to the yoke of demons and to bear the burden of the heaviest sin! How can this be after we have known that the heart of those who worship idols is ashes and their life more worthless than clay, and after we have said, "Our ancestors possessed false idols, and none of them can bring rain"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
We wish to understand the words spoken to Jerusalem with much menace, which run thus: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? Or who will be sorrowful for you? Or who will turn aside to ask after your peace? You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You shall go backward, and I will stretch out my hand against you and destroy you, and I will no longer let you go. And I will scatter them in a dispersion." Then: "I have been made childless." Perplexity has seized me. I take as an illustration a man who has been declared an enemy of the one who reigns upon the earth, because for such a person it is not permitted even to impart mercy, lest anyone seem to give offense to the king who has condemned him. And it is not permitted even to show mercy to such a one; some go still further and do not even show sorrow over him, lest by showing sorrow they seem to be displeased with the sentence passed by the king. If you have grasped this, look with me at the one condemned by God on account of his own many sins, and consider such a person: though there are legions of angels appointed to help the nature of human beings, he is pitied by none. For each of the angels, seeing that the one who has condemned him is God, that the one from whom he has turned away is the Creator, that the nature of the sins is such that the good God was compelled — so to speak — to bring the verdict against the one who has sinned, each of those who see does not spare, does not show sorrow, does not pity, does not turn back to intercede for peace toward such a one.

Let this Jerusalem, then (for so it shall be spoken according to the letter), have sinned against my Jesus, and have done such things, that Jesus should say concerning her: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not. Behold, your house is left to you." Let this Jerusalem be forsaken, as she has been forsaken. Let the angels who ever help Jerusalem — through whom also the law of Moses was ordained, "ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator" — let them forsake Jerusalem and say: her sins have become great, they have killed Jesus, they have laid their hands upon Christ. As long as the sins were still smaller, we could still make request and intercede concerning them, we could spare Jerusalem; who will spare her in this case? "If a man sinning sins against another man, then they shall pray for him; but if he sins against the Lord, who shall pray for him?" "Jerusalem has sinned a sin; therefore she has become an object of tossing." And it is said to this very one first: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?" We do not show sorrow over Jerusalem and over her calamities and over the things that befell all that people; "for by their trespass salvation has come to us, to provoke them to jealousy." Since their trespass became so great a sin that it was said by the voice of the Lord, "Who then will spare you" — I too say to her who killed my Jesus — "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?"

I pass over from the letter — although I have had a road, which the word has given — to each soul that has already been counted worthy to see peace; for after the divine lessons you have become Jerusalem, having formerly been Jebus. The history says that the name of that place was Jebus, and afterward it changed its name and became Jerusalem. Jebus, the children of the Hebrews say, is interpreted "trodden down." Jebus, then, the soul trodden down by the opposing powers, has been changed and become Jerusalem, "Vision of peace." If, then, when you have been changed from Jebus into becoming Jerusalem, you have sinned and "trodden down the Son of God and counted the blood of the new covenant a common thing" (as she did, so also you), and are in grievous sins, it will be said also concerning you: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you?" — if you become such as to betray Jesus. Each of us when he sins, and especially if he sins the greater sins, sins against Jesus. And if he is also an apostate, then all the more does he do to Jesus spiritually the things which Jerusalem did to him bodily. Therefore, "of how much worse punishment do you think he will be counted worthy who has trodden down the Son of God and counted the blood of the covenant a common thing, by which he was sanctified, and has insulted the Spirit of grace?" If you have trodden down the Son of God and insulted the Spirit of grace, who "will spare you? Who will be sorrowful for you? Who will turn aside to ask after the things that make for your peace?" The very Son of God, who asks after the things that make for your peace, the soul of the sinner has betrayed; who is able to intercede, turning back again concerning peace? Knowing, then, that "it is impossible for those who have once been enlightened and have tasted the heavenly gift and have become partakers of the Holy Spirit and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the age to come, and have fallen away, to renew them again to repentance, since they crucify again for themselves the Son of God and put him to open shame" — let us do everything, so that it may not be said also concerning us: "Who will spare you, O Jerusalem? And who will be sorrowful for you? Or who will turn aside to ask after your peace?"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And to each interpretation of Jerusalem what follows will also fit: "You have turned away from me, says the Lord. You shall go backward." That you have turned away from the Son of God, and because of having turned away from the Son of God you have turned away from God — what need is there even to say it? And since Jerusalem in Judea turned away from Christ — from which we must understand all the Jews — for this reason "you shall go backward." For there was a time when she did not go backward, but forward; but now she goes backward, and "they turned in their hearts to Egypt," clearly so that they might go backward. But concerning what "you shall go backward" means, or what it is to reach forward to the things that are ahead, we shall present it thus. The righteous man "reaches forward to the things that are ahead, forgetting the things that are behind." Clearly the one disposed contrary to the righteous man remembers the things behind and does not reach forward to the things that are ahead. But he who remembers the things behind disobeys Jesus who teaches and says: "Let him not turn back to take up his garment"; he disobeys Jesus who says: "Remember Lot's wife"; he disobeys Jesus who says: "No one who has put his hand to the plow and turned back to the things behind is fit for the kingdom of God." And in the law also it is written that the angels said to Lot who had gone out from Sodom: "Do not look around to the things behind, nor stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be swept away with them." And this too has a meaning worthy of an angelic spirit: "Do not look around to the things behind" — ever reach forward to the things ahead. You have left Sodom, do not turn to Sodom. You have left vice and sin, do not turn back to it, "nor stand in all the surrounding country." And even if you keep the first commandment which says, "Do not look around to the things behind," it does not suffice you for salvation, unless you also hear the second commandment which says, "Nor stand in all the surrounding country." For one who has begun to make progress must not stand in the surrounding country of Sodom, even if he has passed beyond Sodom, but having passed beyond standing in the surrounding country he must be saved to the mountain, according to the "Do not look around to the things behind, nor stand in all the surrounding country; escape to the mountain, lest you be swept away with them." If you wish not to be swept away with the Sodomites, never turn to the things behind, nor stand in the surrounding country of Sodom, nor be anywhere else than at the mountain; for there alone is it possible to be saved. And the mountain is the Lord Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Physicians of bodies, being present with the sick and always devoting themselves to the care of the ailing according to the intent of the medical art, look upon dreadful things and touch loathsome ones; from the misfortunes of others they reap their own griefs, and their life is always in the midst of hardship. For they are never with the healthy, but always with the wounded, with those who have festering sores, with those full of pus, of fevers, of manifold diseases. And if anyone wishes to make ready the practice of medicine, he will not be indignant nor neglect the intent of the art which he has taken up, whenever he is among such people as we have described.

I have spoken this preface because the prophets too are, as it were, physicians of souls, and they always spend their time where those who need healing are; for "it is not the healthy who have need of a physician, but those who are ill." And what physicians suffer at the hands of the intemperate sick, this the prophets and the teachers also suffer at the hands of those who do not wish to be healed. For thence they are hated, as though they gave orders contrary to the preference of the desire of the sick, as though they hindered from luxury and pleasure those who, even in their sicknesses, wish not to receive what befits their sicknesses. So the intemperate among the sick flee from their physicians, often even reviling them and speaking evil of them and doing every possible thing that an enemy might do to an enemy. For these people forget that the physicians come as friends, since they look only at the toilsomeness of the regimen, at the toilsomeness of the physicians' stroke with the iron, and not at the end that comes after the toil; and they hate them as fathers of toils only, and not of toils that bring those who are treated to health.

That people, then, was sick; manifold diseases were in the people that had been called the people of God. God sent them physicians, the prophets. One of the physicians was Jeremiah too; he reproved the sinners, wishing to turn back those who were doing evil. But they, when they ought to have listened to what was said, accused the prophet, and accused him before judges who were much like themselves. And the prophet was always in lawsuits at the hands of those who, so far as his prophecy was concerned, were being healed, but who, because of their own disobedience, were not being healed. Concerning these things he says at one point: "And I said, I will not speak, nor will I name the name of the Lord. And it became like a burning fire, blazing in my bones, and I am unstrung on every side and cannot bear it." And at another point he says, seeing himself always brought to trial, reviled, accused, borne false witness against: "Woe is me, mother, as what have you borne me?" He said "a man" not judging but "being judged," and not passing judgment but "being disputed against by all the earth." And since the sick did not listen to him when he counseled them well and after the manner of a physician, he says, "I did not profit." And since, when he was lending the spiritual silver pieces, those to whom he spoke were unwilling to listen, that they might be profited by what they heard, he says, "Neither did anyone owe me, nor did I owe."

But I have said these things by way of anticipation, before I expound the words "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me." For the text is twofold: in most copies it reads "I did not profit, nor did anyone profit me," but in the most accurate ones, which agree with the Hebrew, it reads "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me." One must therefore both expound what is worn smooth by use and current in the churches, and not leave unexpounded what comes from the Hebrew Scriptures. He was proclaiming the word, then, and no one accepted what was said. Like a physician he was expending his remedies, though the sick were intemperate and fulfilling their own desires. As if he too were saying, "I did not profit, nor did anyone profit me." Perhaps there is a reciprocal feeling, on account of the love-toward-humanity of the one profited toward the one who profited him, so that the speaker too comes to be profited, since "blessed is the one who speaks into the ears of those who hear." This profit, then, a teacher might receive from hearers who advance and are made better; he might be profited by having fruits in them. ⟨Not having this from the Jews, Jeremiah says:⟩ "No one profited me." For if the speaker ought to have fruit in himself, but the hearer misconstrues and remains outside of what is said, then it is said, "No single one profited me"; since he does not have this profit which he would have received from the hearer, once profited, becoming a cause of advancement and blessedness for the one who profited him. And besides, everyone who teaches, by the very act of teaching, the more intelligent the learner is, is profited in the things he teaches, in the things he learns. And speakers become better regarding the lessons they hand on, when the hearers are intelligent and do not simply accept, but test in return and question and examine the intent of what is said. ⟨Neither, then, did I profit, nor did anyone profit me.⟩

But since another exposition is also necessary on account of the more accurate copies, which read thus: "I did not owe, nor did anyone owe me," we shall expound the saying as it stands thus also. The one who renders to all their debts—to whom fear, fear; to whom the tax, the tax; to whom the tribute, the tribute; to whom the honor, the honor—and who renders to all their dues, so as not to owe the dues toward anyone, honoring ⟨parents⟩ as parents, so to speak, brothers as brothers, sons as sons, bishops as bishops, presbyters as presbyters, deacons as deacons, believers as believers, catechumens as catechumens—if he renders all the dues, he did not owe. But if he owes indeed to do a due, and has not done it, he cannot say, "I did not owe"; for owing, he did not render it. How then shall I expound also "nor did anyone owe me"? I indeed was lending and wished to give the spiritual riches, but they turned away from what was said and did not present themselves receptive, so as to owe; therefore no single one owed me. For who accepted what was said, so that from accepting it he might become a debtor of what he heard, and be required, as a debtor of what was said, to pay the interest? It is better, then, in this respect for the hearer to receive rational silver from the speaker and to owe, than, not accepting nor receiving, not even to owe. For "nor did any single one owe me" is set among reproaches.

As for "Woe is me, mother, as what a man have you begotten me, being judged and disputed against in all the earth"—I do not think it so fitting for the other prophets to say this as for Jeremiah; for most of the prophets, after certain periods of time, after their wickedness, after their sins, changed and began to prophesy, but Jeremiah prophesies from childhood. And it is possible to give an example from the writings. Isaiah did not hear "Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, and before you came forth from the mother's womb I sanctified you, I have set you as a prophet unto the nations"; nor did he say, "I do not know how to speak, because I am too young," but when he saw the vision recorded in his prophecy, he saw and said: "Woe is me, wretched that I am, because having unclean lips I dwell in the midst of a people having unclean lips, and I have seen with my eyes the King, the Lord of Sabaoth," "and there was sent," he says, "to me one of the Seraphim, and he touched my lips and said: Behold, I have taken away your iniquities, and this will cleanse your sins." After the sins, then, which he had formerly committed, Isaiah later became worthy of the Holy Spirit and prophesied. And in another you would find something similar. But not so Jeremiah; for while still in swaddling-clothes, adorned with the prophetic Spirit, he prophesied from childhood; wherefore he said (for I expound first the common sense): "Woe is me, mother, as what a man have you begotten me, being judged and disputed against by all the earth?"

But one of those before me applied himself to the passage, saying that he spoke these things not to his bodily mother, but to the mother who gives birth to prophets. And who gives birth to prophets but the wisdom of God? He said, then, "Woe is me, mother," "as what have you borne me," O wisdom? And the children of wisdom are recorded in the Gospel too: "And wisdom sends out her children." It has been said, then: "Woe is me, mother," my wisdom, "as what a man have you borne me, being judged"—who am I, that I have been begotten to such a degree, that I should be judged, that I should be disputed against because of the reproofs, because of the rebukes, because of the teaching directed to all who are upon the earth? If Jeremiah says these things, "as what a man have you borne me, being judged and disputed against by all the earth," I cannot expound the "by all the earth"; for Jeremiah was not disputed against by all the earth. Or shall we, forcing the matter, take "by all the earth" instead of "by all Judea"? For his prophecy, as he prophesied then, did not reach unto all the earth. But perhaps, just as in countless other cases we have shown that Jeremiah is spoken in place of our Lord Jesus Christ, so here too we shall say. At the beginning I noted the "Behold, I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to root up and to pull down and to destroy and to build and to plant." This Jeremiah did not do. But Jesus Christ rooted up the sinful kingdoms of the [earth] and pulled down the buildings of wickedness, and made, in place of those kingdoms, righteousness and truth to reign in our souls. As, then, those things were more fittingly to be referred to Christ than to Jeremiah, so I think many other things also, including these.

First we must speak concerning the "Woe is me," whether, on account of its ill-omened form, the Savior—who also pronounces others wretched—can say the "Woe is me." We shall establish from acknowledged sayings, which fit no one else than the Savior, in what manner he also wept over Jerusalem; and the "Woe is me" is the voice of one weeping. And it stands in the Gospel that when he saw Jerusalem he wept over it and said: "Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you, how often have I wished to gather together your children," and what follows. And clearly these words too were spoken by the Savior in the "Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at the harvest, and like a gleaning at the vintage, when there is no ear of grain to eat the first-fruits. Woe is my soul, for the reverent has perished from the earth, and there is no one upright among men. All are brought to trial for bloodshed." For he came [as one gathering stubble] into the harvest, that he might reap, and he finds many sinners and says: "Woe is me, for I have become like one who gathers stubble at the harvest." He came to gather in the fruit of life among men; he finds many sins in us, and therefore he says: "and like a gleaning at the vintage, when there is no ear of grain to eat the first-fruits." He says something similar to these things elsewhere too, speaking to the Father: "What profit is there in my blood, in my going down to corruption?" What such great thing did I profit men? What worthy of the blood which I poured out on their behalf have they done? "What profit is there in my blood, in my going down" from the heavens? I went down, I came to the earth, I gave myself over to corruption, I bore a human body; what worthy of these things has been accomplished among men? "What profit is there in my blood, in my going down to corruption? Will dust confess to you, or declare your truth?" Such, then, is also the first thing spoken here by the Savior, the "Woe is me, mother, as what a man have you borne me?" Not insofar as he is God does the Savior say the "Woe is me, mother," but insofar as he is man, as in the prophet: "Woe is my soul, for the reverent has perished from the earth." And the soul was human; therefore it was also troubled, therefore it was also exceedingly sorrowful. But the Word who was in the beginning with God is not troubled; that one would not say the "Woe is me." For neither does the Word admit death, but it is the human element that admitted this, as we have often established.

"As what a man have you borne me, being judged and disputed against in all the earth?" If you look for me at the martyrs everywhere being judged and standing before the judges in each church, you will see in what manner Jesus Christ is judged in each of the martyrs; for he himself is the one being judged in those who bear witness to the truth. And you will be persuaded to accept this when you see that he says it is not you who are in prison when you are in prison, but himself; not you who are hungry when you are hungry, but himself; not you who are thirsty, but himself. "I was in prison and you came to me. I was hungry and you gave me to eat, I was thirsty and you gave me to drink." Therefore even if a Christian is judged not for anything else, not for his own sins, but because he is a Christian, it is Christ who is judged. In all the earth, then, Christ Jesus is judged; and as often, then, as a Christian is judged, it is Christ who is judged; and not only in these law-courts, but suppose a Christian is slandered, accused concerning something [as is bound to happen], then too Christ is unjustly judged.

And still further you will understand in this way how "he is judged and disputed against in all the earth." Who, then, does not judge the Christian word? Who of the nations, even simply, does not examine it? Who of the Jews does not say the things about Christians? Who of the Greeks? Who of the philosophers? Who of the common folk? Everywhere Jesus is judged and tried; and by some he is condemned, but by others he is not condemned. If he is not condemned, he becomes accepted; you open the windows to him, he enters in to you; you believe in him, he dines with you. But if you do not accept him when you hear about Christianity, you have done nothing else than condemned Jesus as lying, as having deceived men, as not speaking the truth, through not having believed the word which he teaches. "As what a man have you borne me, being judged and disputed against in all the earth?" As many as utterly disbelieve, condemn him; but as many as do not disbelieve but are in doubt about him, dispute concerning him. Jesus suffers two things among men: by the unbelievers he is condemned, but by the double-minded he is disputed. If you bear "the image of the heavenly," having put off "the image of the earthy," you are not earth condemning him, nor are you earth in which he is condemned, no longer are you earth disputing him.

"My strength has failed among those who curse me." The apostle says concerning the Savior that "he was crucified out of weakness." And the prophet too says things similar to these in the "Lord, who has believed our report? And to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed? We announced before him as a child, as a root in a thirsty ground; we saw him, and he had no form nor beauty, but his form was without honor, failing beyond the sons of men. A man in a stroke and in toil and knowing how to bear weakness, because his face has been turned away from dishonor; he was dishonored and not esteemed. This one bears our iniquities and grieves for us, and we accounted him to be in toil and in a stroke and in affliction. But he was wounded because of our iniquities, and has been weakened because of our sins; the chastisement of our peace was upon him, by his bruise we were healed." Therefore he took up the weakness of our sins and bore us and came to those who curse him, and his strength failed among those who curse him as he came down from the heavens. For as soon as he took up the form of the servant, he also emptied himself, as the apostle said that "he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." "My strength has failed," then, he says, "among those who curse me."

Let us see whether, the Word himself granting it, we can also say something clearer beyond what has been said with regard to "My strength has failed among those who curse me." "There was the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." "The true light" is the Son of God, "which enlightens every man coming into the world." And whoever is rational partakes of the true light, and every man is rational. Of all men, then, who partake of reason, in some the strength of the Word has grown, but in some it fails. If you look at a passionate and sinful soul, you will see there the strength of the Word failing; but if you look at a holy and righteous soul, you will see the strength of the Word bearing fruit day by day, and you will fit what was said about Jesus to the righteous. For not in himself alone did "Jesus advance in wisdom and stature and grace with God and men," but also in each of those who receive advancement in wisdom, stature, and grace, "Jesus advances in wisdom, stature, and grace with God and men." The Word, then, the Son of God, who is in the one who said "Woe is me, mother," and what follows, says: "My strength has failed among those who curse me." Whoever curses the Word, he straightway receives the punishment for cursing the Word, for finding fault with the teaching of Jesus; for the strength of Jesus fails in such a one, and there is no strength of the Word in him. As again, on the contrary, if you bless Jesus and accept him, his strength suffers the opposite of what it suffered among those who curse him; for as there it failed among those who curse, so here it grows among those who bless.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
Those who call the prophets blessed, and who by calling them blessed pray to have their portion with the prophets, gather from the prophetic words the choicest features of their prophecy. Seeking, then, they might be persuaded—if they should live according to these things (even if it should turn out hard for them in this life to imitate the prophetic life)—that they will attain rest and blessedness together with the prophets. Now it is possible from many sources to gather the choice qualities of the prophets: their freedom, their vigor, their wakefulness, their alertness—that they were not anxious when they found themselves in dire circumstances, because of their freedom, their only concern being to reprove, to convert, as prophets do, by speaking the word of God with boldness, rebuking the sinners, even though those being reproved seemed to have great power. But even if it is possible to do this from every source, let us look also at the passages read today.

The prophet reproved many, and the prophet spoke to many; for he indeed lived among people who had become sinners, as is clear from the fact that the captivity occurred in his days. Having reproved many, and being judged by many, he utters words of this kind.

For first let us look at it from the prophetic word, and then also according to the anagogical sense, if we first take up the vigor and freedom and power and boldness of a prophet. "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a man—one contending in judgment and disputed with in all the earth!" O mother, why have you borne me a man contending in judgment against all who are upon the earth, and being disputed with against all who are upon the earth? For it was set before this prophet, and before Isaiah, and before the rest, to fulfill the prophetic office: to teach, to reprove, and to convert. It was therefore set before this prophet also to distinguish, to reprove, being able to contend in judgment and to be contended with among the sinners, to reprove the sins of the people. And as for all that the members of the people did to them, what need is there even to speak of it? One they stoned, one they sawed asunder, one they killed "between the temple and the altar," and this one, when he reproved them, they threw into a pit of mire. And above all our Savior did this, and better indeed than they, inasmuch as he is Lord of the prophets. For indeed, though he himself was scourged and crucified and handed over by the Jews or by the teachers of the Jews and the ruler of the people, he said, "Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites"; and he adds in each case "woe" and "because of this" such-and-such and such-and-such. Let us therefore also, if we are eager for the beatitudes of the prophets, do these same things, so that, because of speaking and because of being brought to judgment against many people, we too may say, "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a man—one contending in judgment and disputed with in all the earth!"

This prophetic saying can more properly be referred to the Savior. For grant that the prophet says this—but he will not say it truly, but perhaps hyperbolically; for he was not disputed with against all the earth. But if I come to my Savior and Lord, and especially because of "he shall come to judgment" and "so that you may be justified in your words, and may prevail when you are judged," I shall see that my Savior and Lord is going to stand before the Father, being judged together with all of us human beings. And he is judged together with all human beings. I say: he is judged, he too is examined, and he stood as one vindicating the truth, yet not as an accuser. "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a man—one contending in judgment and disputed with in all the earth!" A prophet cannot say "in all the earth."

But some who love our Lord grow indignant and say that it is not the Savior who speaks, that the voice is not fitting for the Son of God. But it must be shown that "Woe is me, mother" is not foreign to the Son of God. "My soul is sorrowful even unto death," and "My soul is troubled," and, like the things said in the prophets, so also here: "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a man—one contending in judgment and disputed with in all the earth"; or when the gleaning has perished so as to find no cluster: "Woe is me, soul, for the devout man has perished from the earth, and there is none upright among men." Who is it there that says, "Woe is me, for I have become as one gathering stubble at harvest"? For did the prophet gather, and does he wish to gather? Does the prophet indeed possess a field? But it belongs to no one to gather all things from the harvest and from what is sown, except to the Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. Since, then, there are many falls among the nations, but also among us, speaking of the sins he says, "Woe is me, for I have become as one gathering stubble." Let each of us examine himself: is he an ear of grain? Will the Son of God find in him anything to gather or to reap? We shall find that some of us are blasted by the wind; and even if we still have a little, two or three grains within ourselves, our sins upon us are many. Seeing, then, also the churches that bear the name, filled with sinners, he says, "Woe is me, for I have become as one gathering stubble at harvest and as a gleaning at vintage." He came seeking fruit on the vine; for each of us is planted . . . and as a vine "in a fertile place," and "he brought over a vine out of Egypt," "but I planted you a fruitful vine, wholly a true one." He comes, he seeks somehow to gather the vintage; he finds a certain gleaning and a few clusters, neither flourishing nor many. Which of us has clusters of virtue? Which of us has offspring of God? "O Lord our God, how wonderful is your name in all the earth."

Let these things be said by me as it were in a digression upon "Woe is me, mother." That it is not foreign to the divinity of our Savior, who beholds the sins of men, now to say "woe"—the Savior speaking not insofar as he is God but insofar as he is man, not insofar as he is Wisdom but insofar as he is soul—I adduced that prophetic saying: "Woe is me, soul, for the devout man has perished from the earth, and there is none upright among men." The blessed soul came into human life, took up a body on behalf of men. If it sees the sins, it says to the Father, "What profit is there in my blood, when I go down to corruption? Shall the dust confess to you?" But let him not say "woe" over us; let the angels of heaven not say "woe" over us. When our Savior says "woe," they too will say "woe"; for they are not better than our Savior, and they too see our faults. But blessed are those over whom the angels will not say "woe," but are called blessed; for "there is joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine who have no need of repentance." Let these things be said by way of consolation. "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a one!" What mother does he mean? Among women, can he not mean both the soul and Mary? But if anyone accepts the saying, "Just now my mother the Holy Spirit took me, and carried me up to the great mountain, Tabor," and what follows, he can see his mother. "Woe is me, mother, that you have borne me such a man—one contending in judgment and disputed with in all the earth!" He is contended with in all the earth and disputed with, and he is going to say to each one: I did such-and-such, and my dispensation performed such-and-such, and for your salvation I endured. When the Savior says these things, what shall we do? For he is going to be disputed with in all the earth.

I wish to look at what follows. It can be referred, according to one interpretation, both to the prophet and to the Savior. Let us look also at what follows: "I have not been in debt, nor has anyone been in debt to me." "The ruler of this world comes, but he has nothing in me." And truly he was not in debt. But each of us is a debtor by his sins, and is a debtor holding a bond of indebtedness. After his bond was wiped out, † how many bonds have they made? "He who committed no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth," made no bond. But what of "no one has been in debt to me"? How shall we interpret, in the case of the Savior, "no one has been in debt to me"? Even if we read it thus, yet one must also know that the majority of the copies of the edition of the Seventy do not have it thus, and later, examining also the remaining editions, we recognized that it is a scribal error. And yet to me "not even one"; so that "not even one" was in debt to him—he forgave all men their debts. "There were two debtors to a certain creditor: one owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. When they had nothing to repay, he freely forgave them both." Do you wish to see the two debtors, the one owing the five hundred and the one owing the fifty? From two peoples they have believed in God: the people from the Jews, disbelieving in Christ, owes the fifty; and perhaps we from the nations, who had become the most impious of all, owe the five hundred—concerning whom is also said what is said about that harlot who repented. And yet someone might say, how are the five hundred referred to her? From the words "and what sort of woman it is who is touching him," to which he said to Simon, "There were two debtors to a certain creditor. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty," and what follows. These things because of "I have not been in debt, nor has anyone been in debt to me," which it was necessary to set before you. "I have not been in debt, nor has anyone been in debt to me; my strength has failed among those who curse me." For even if "he died from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "So be it, Lord, when they set straight their way; did I not stand by you in the time of their evils?" What is "So be it, Lord"? Let the one who is able gather such a meaning for himself. [The "So be it"—] "Master, Lord, when they set straight their way"—may the strength that fails among those who curse come to be, when, having repented after speaking evil of me, they turn to the straight path and travel it. "So be it, Master, when they set straight their way; did I not stand by you?" Then he pleads his cause concerning those who speak evil of him, saying: "Did I not stand by you in the time of their evils?" He stood by the Father, ⟨being a propitiation for our sins,⟩ and interceded concerning them in that very time of our evils. For he did not stand by after the time of our evils, but "while we were yet sinners Christ died for us"—"Did I not stand by you in the time of their evils, in the time of their afflictions, for good against the enemy?" And in the time of their affliction, he says, of the affliction against the enemy, I stood by you on their behalf. And who is the enemy but "our adversary the devil," who afflicted us? And clearly in the time of that one's enmity against men, our Savior stood by the Father and made petition concerning our captivity, that we might be ransomed and rescued from the enemy. Let the Savior, or the prophet, have said these things; for the prophet too can have said such things and have prayed on behalf of the people in the "time of their evils."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Upon these things [what] does God answer to the people that was accused by the prophet or by Christ, and he says these things to it: "Iron and a covering of bronze is your strength"—hard, unyielding, not to be hammered out. "Iron and a covering of bronze is your strength," that is, your strength is something cutting and dividing, a strength not existing for good.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And I will give your treasures for plunder, as an exchange for all your sins." What "treasures" of the sinners does God give "for plunder," and give them "as an exchange for all their sins"? Is it perchance those treasured up for themselves on earth? For each of men treasures up: if he is base, upon earth; but if he is refined, in heaven, as we were taught from the Gospel. Or does he say to that people, that I am about to give your treasures for plunder because of your sins? What treasures of that people were given for plunder? Behold, one of the treasures is Jeremiah, another treasure is Isaiah, a treasure was Moses too. These treasures God took from that people, and through Christ—who said, "The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and shall be given to a nation producing its fruits"—he gave to us.

"I will give," then, "because of your sins your treasures for plunder." And he gave the treasures of that people to us; ⟨for first those were entrusted with the oracles of God,⟩ then after them we were entrusted, the oracles of God having been taken from them and given to us. And we say that the "The kingdom of God shall be taken away from you and shall be given to a nation producing its fruits" was spoken by the Savior and has been fulfilled. Not that the Scripture was taken from them, but that now they no longer have the law and the prophets, in that they do not perceive the mind that is in them. For they have the books, but how has the kingdom of God been taken from them? The mind of the Scriptures has been taken from them. No longer is a legal or prophetic exposition preserved among them. But they are people reading and not understanding; for through the coming of Christ there has been fulfilled the "I said to that people: With hearing you shall hear and shall not understand, and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive. For the heart of this people has grown thick." There has been fulfilled also what was said by Isaiah, that "the Lord will remove from Judea and from Jerusalem the mighty man and the mighty woman, the giant and the man of war, the judge and the prophet and the diviner and the wise master-builder and the intelligent hearer." All these things God removed from them and gave, if indeed we receive them, to us who are from the nations. These things follow from the "And your treasures I will give for plunder."

"As an exchange for all your sins and in all your borders." As if he said: because of your sins that have reached upon all your borders; for there is no border of that people which has not been filled with sins. And how was not every border of theirs going to be filled with sins [upon them], since, so far as lay in them, they killed righteousness, if Christ is righteousness; killed wisdom, if Christ is wisdom; killed truth, if Christ is truth? For through having condemned the Son of God to death, they cast away and destroyed all these things. And my Lord Jesus, having risen from the dead, no longer appeared to those who killed him; for we do not have in the history that he appeared to those who killed him, but he appeared, risen from the dead, only to those who believe.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And I will make you a slave among all your enemies in the land which you did not know." That people has been enslaved among its enemies, and has come to be in the land which it did not know. "Because a fire has been kindled out of my wrath; it shall be burned upon you."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
After these things and the words of the threats spoken to the people, the one who prayed above completes his prayer and joins to the aforesaid these words: "You know, Lord; remember me and visit me, and acquit me from those who persecute me, not unto long-suffering." And let the prophet say these things, persecuted by those he reproved, hated by those who cannot contain the truth; for he became an enemy to his hearers by speaking the truth to them. And let our Savior too say these same things, who was also persecuted by the people and says: "not unto long-suffering." What is the "not unto long-suffering"? You have always been long-suffering toward the people over their sins, but over the things dared against me do not be long-suffering. And truly God was not long-suffering. If you examine the times of the passion and of the fall of Jerusalem and of the razing of the city, and in what manner God abandoned that people, since they killed Christ, you will see that he no longer used long-suffering toward the people. And if you wish, listen: from the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar to the razing of the temple, forty-two years are completed. For it was necessary that some little time be granted for repentance, especially for the sake of those from the people who were going to believe from the signs and wonders that would be worked by the apostles.

"Know that for your sake I have received reproach from those who set at nought your words." Let it be the prophet who speaks, both the one who was despised for the things he said, set at nought by the sinners; for he himself says: "I have continued being mocked." He was therefore reproached by those who set at nought the words spoken through him by God, and he prays, on account of having been reproached, to be helped by God, saying: "Know that for your sake I have received reproach from those who set at nought your words; make an end of them." Let the prophet say it — but the "make an end of them" is more fittingly said by the Savior; for a consummation came upon Jerusalem and the people, on account of the things that happened out of the people's plot against our Savior.

After this it is necessary, on account of the many things the prophets suffered while reproving and serving as ambassadors of the word and speaking the things commanded by God, to remind the hearers concerning their life and their promises and our own resolve, so that, as far as is possible for us, if we wish to have rest together with the prophets, we may emulate the works of the prophets. And what I say is this: often in our prayers we say, "God Almighty, grant our portion with the prophets, grant our portion with the apostles of your Christ, that we may also be found with Christ himself." But saying these things we do not perceive what we are praying; for in effect we are saying: grant us to suffer what the prophets suffered, grant that we too be hated as the prophets were hated, grant us such words for which we shall be hated, grant that we fall into as many hardships as the apostles did. For to say, "Grant me a portion with the prophets," when one has not suffered the things of the prophets and is not willing to suffer them, is unjust. To say, "Grant me a portion with the apostles," when one is not willing, out of the disposition of Paul, to say truthfully, "in labors more abundant, in stripes more abundant, in prisons more frequent, in deaths often," and what follows — this is the most unjust of all. If, then, we wish to come to be with the prophets, consider the lives of the prophets, that out of reproving, out of rebuking, out of chastising, they were brought to trial, put on judgment, condemned. "They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, they were tempted, they died by the slaughter of the sword, they wandered about in sheepskins, in goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, ill-treated, wandering in deserts," while there were many synagogues of the Jews; and these men were "wandering in deserts and in mountains and in caves and in the holes of the earth." What, then, is strange, if one wishing to emulate the prophetic life, reproving, chastising the sinner, is spoken evil of, is hated, is plotted against? Just as also in the present case it was necessary that such a thing should occur in the Church of God. The one who was condemned was condemned; a certain man who was seated was doing such things; there needed to be an ecclesiastical vindication, and it has come about; the one entrusted with the task has done the work he ought to have done. That man goes about speaking evil of the one who vindicated the truth. But let us not do this; let us not lend our ears to those who, because of having been cast out, speak evil of the one who cast them out or of the one who cast a concurring vote. Those who indeed, even when the injustice has been reproved and has taken place. The wondrous apostles, being insulted in ten thousand ways for the sake of the truth, say: "I take pleasure in weaknesses, in insults and necessities, in persecutions and distresses, for Christ's sake." Only let it be mine, when insulted, to know that I am insulted for no other reason than for Christ; when brought into necessities, to know that the ground of the necessities is Christ.
