Let it be mine, when reviled, to know that the pretext of the reviling is none other than that I vindicate the truth and serve as ambassador on behalf of the things written, so that all things may be done according to the word of God — for this reason I am blasphemed. Let all of us, then, with all our power, hasten toward the prophetic life, toward the apostolic life, not fleeing the troublesome; for if an athlete flees the troublesome part of the contest, he will not receive the sweetness of the crown.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And your word shall be to me for gladness." It is not now, but "shall be"; for since at present your word is to me for imprisonments, for trials, for troubles, for defamations, for pains — yet the end of these shall be gladness. "And your word shall be to me for gladness and joy of my heart, because your name has been called upon me, Lord Almighty." And if Christ says it, the name of the Father has been called upon him.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"I did not sit in the assembly of them when they made sport." If ever the prophet saw the assembly not of those in earnest but of those making sport, he fled from being gathered together rather than hastened toward the gathering of those making sport. You must, then, understand the difference between an assembly of those making sport and of those in earnest. This assembly is earnest and does all things with earnestness and things worthy of earnestness, and according to the saying: the word is earnestness, the life is earnestness, and altogether the assembly is not of those making sport, but of those in earnest. But whenever the assembly, forsaking the earnestness about necessary things, gives its leisure to the playthings of this age and to the playthings that come from wickedness, it becomes an assembly of those making sport. This one, then, says: "I did not sit in the assembly of them when they made sport, but I was in awe before the presence of your hand." Two things being set before me — to sit in the assembly of those making sport and to give offense to you the God and not to please you, or to rise up from the assembly of those making sport and to do the things that were dear to you — I chose rather to rise up from the assembly of those making sport and to be a friend to you, than, doing the contrary, to become an enemy to your blessedness. "I did not sit in the assembly of them when they made sport, but I was in awe before the presence of your hand." And our Savior did not sit "in the assembly of them when they made sport," but rose up away from them. And a sign that the Savior had risen up from the assembly of those making sport is his having said: "Your house is left to you desolate." For the word of God has forsaken the assembly of the Jews and has made for himself another assembly and church, the one from the nations.

"I sat alone." And here too the words are ordered by design. When there is a multitude of sinners and they do not bear the righteous man living righteously, it is nothing strange that one fleeing the assembly of wickedness should imitate him who said, "I sat alone," and should imitate also Elijah who says, "Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have dug down your altars, and I am left utterly alone, and they seek my life, to take it." And perhaps too, if you examine "I sat alone" more deeply, you will find a certain sense worthy of prophetic depth. Whenever we imitate the life of the many, so that it is not withdrawn and better and select beyond the many, I cannot say, "I sat alone," but: I sat with many. But when my life becomes hard to imitate, so that I become so great that no one is near to me in character, in word, in deeds, in wisdom, then I can say, from being alone in being such and from no one imitating me, "I sat alone." It is possible, then, even for you who are not a presbyter and are not a bishop nor honored with any ecclesiastical honor, to say this — to emulate "I sat alone" and to take up a life such that you may say, "I sat alone." "Because I was filled with bitterness." If "narrow and afflicted is the way" that leads to life, you must be filled with bitterness in this life; you can enjoy nothing sweet. Or do you not know that your feast is made with bitter herbs? For when you feast, it says, "you shall eat unleavened bread upon bitter herbs." What the word means when it says that the one feasting to God must eat "unleavened bread upon bitter herbs" must be considered. The unleavened bread the apostle has expounded — the interpretation is not mine; but that which follows in the interpretation must necessarily be close to the apostolic exposition. The apostle expounded the things concerning the unleavened bread, saying: "Let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." It is fitting, then, to render the account concerning the bitter herbs in a manner following upon the unleavened bread's being of sincerity and truth. Have sincerity and truth, and bitter herbs will be yours, and you will eat with bitter herbs the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth — like Paul. Since he ate the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth, he also ate bitter herbs. How did he eat bitter herbs? By saying, "Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?" How did he eat bitter herbs? "In labor and toil, and in watchings often, in hunger and thirst, besides the things that are external." The law, then, said: "You shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs"; and it did not say: you shall eat unleavened bread with bitter herbs until you are filled, as has been said concerning certain other things: "You shall eat and be filled." But the prophet intensifies it further, saying that I did not eat bitterness, but "I was filled with bitterness"; as far as was possible I partook of bitter matters, so that I partook of bitter herbs in fullest measure.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Why do those who hate me prevail?" He had many troubles; he suffered from those who did not wish to hear the truth, and those men were more powerful than he here in this age, since the kingdom of God is not from this age, but from the better regions, as the Savior says: "If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would have striven, that I should not be delivered to the Jews." Those, then, who grieved the prophet prevailed over him in this world. For that they do prevail, look at the martyrs. The judge sits giving judgment and living luxuriously in the tribunal; the Christian, in whom Christ is being judged, was filled with bitterness and is overpowered by the unjust man and is condemned.

"My wound is firm, whence shall I be healed?" Those who prevail over me strike me, and my wound is firm. Whether he prophesies the cross of the Lord (for the cross is a firm wound, so far as concerns those who crucify him), or whether it is said concerning all the righteous in whom a firm wound is received, or whether you hear this also of the prophet (for he too suffered the things recorded in the prophecy) — it admits the same sense according to the expression that says: "My wound is firm." "Whence shall I be healed?" And if the Savior says, "Whence shall I be healed," he prophesies the resurrection from the dead after the firm wound; and if it is taken of the righteous man too, after the wounds there comes healing again. "Becoming, it became to me as deceitful water that has no faithfulness"; for the wound does not remain, but passes away.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Therefore thus says the Lord: If you return, then I will restore you." These things again are said to each one whom God shall exhort to return to him. And a mystery seems to me to be indicated here in the "I will restore you." No one is restored to a place in which he has in no way ever been, but the restoration is to what is one's own. For instance, if a limb of mine becomes dislocated, the physician tries to make a restoration of what is dislocated. When someone comes to be outside his homeland, whether justly or unjustly, and then recovers the ability to be again in the homeland according to the laws, he has been restored to his own homeland. Understand the same for me also in the case of a soldier who has been cast out from his own ranks and is restored. He says, then, here to us who have turned away, that if we return, he will restore us. For the end of the promise is such, as is written in the Acts of the Apostles in the words, "until the times of the restoration of all things which God spoke by the mouth of his holy prophets from of old," in Christ Jesus, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
It is recorded in the Gospel according to Matthew that our Savior came alongside the Sea of Galilee and saw "Simon and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea; for they were fishermen." Then the text says that the Savior, seeing them, said: "Come after me, and I will make you fishers of men. And they left their nets and followed him." And Jesus made them take up the work of fishing for men. And "he found two other brothers, James the son of Zebedee and John his brother, in the boat with their father, mending their nets; and these too he called" to the same skill, and he made these also fishers of men. And if anyone has considered those who have from God the grace of a word woven together like nets and composed out of the sacred Scriptures like a casting-net, so that the mesh is thrown around the souls of the hearers, and has considered too that this is done skillfully according to the art, he will see in a certain manner that not only then but also now our Savior sends out fishers of men, having trained them, so that we may be able to come up from the sea and to flee its bitter waves.

But those fish, the soulless ones, when they come up in the dragnets and in the casting-nets and in the nets or on the hooks, die a death in which life does not succeed death. But the one caught by the fishermen of Jesus and brought up from the sea also himself dies, yet he dies to the world, he dies to sin, and after dying to the world and to sin he is made alive by the Word of God and takes up another life. As if, for the sake of argument, you could conceive of the soul of the fish changing after it goes out from the body of the fish and becoming something better than a fish (I have taken an illustration; let no one seize on it as a pretext † as though he had not heard), then you will conceive of something of this sort. You have come up from the sea, having fallen under the nets of the disciples of Jesus; having gone out, you change your soul, you are no longer a fish spending its time in the salty waves of the sea, but immediately your soul changes and is transformed and becomes something better and more divine than what it was before. And that it is transformed and changed, hear Paul saying: "But we all, with unveiled face beholding as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord." And when he has been transformed, this fish caught by the fishermen of Jesus, leaving behind his haunts in the sea, makes his haunts in the mountains, so that he no longer has need of the fishermen who bring him up from the sea, but of certain others, who are named hunters, who hunt "from every mountain and from every hill."

Having therefore come up from the sea and been caught in the nets of the disciples of Jesus, change from the sea, forget it, come to the mountains, the prophets, and to the hills, the righteous, and make your haunts there, so that afterward, when the time of your departure comes upon you, you may be hunted by the hunters. And who would these be but those appointed over receiving the souls that are on the hills, those not lying below? And see whether the prophet does not cry out mystically in saying these things and presenting this meaning in the words: "Behold, I send many fishermen, says the Lord, and they shall fish for them; and after this I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt them upon every mountain and upon every hill."

If, then, you wish to be caught by the hunters, see that you do not make your haunts in the hollows, nor spend your time somewhere below, but seek out the mountains. Go up to the mountain where Jesus was transfigured, go up to the mountain onto which "seeing the crowds Jesus went up," and the disciples followed him, where "opening his mouth he taught, saying: Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven," and the beatitudes that follow these.

And it is not permitted for these hunters to catch from anywhere else than from the mountains and the hills and from the clefts of the rocks. For these three things are spoken of in the prophet: "For I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt them upon every mountain and upon every hill and from the clefts of the rocks." From where, then, shall I understand the rocks and the clefts in the rocks? I come to Exodus, I seek to find a trace of an account of the clefts of the rocks, I find Moses there wishing to know God, and God promising to him and saying: "Behold, I will place you in a hole of the rock, and you shall behold my back parts; but my face shall not be seen by you." If you understand the rock there and see there the hole in the rock, he who sees beholds God through the hole in the rock, you will see also the many rocks and their clefts. Who, then, is that one rock? "And the rock was Christ"; "for they drank from a spiritual rock that followed them," and "he set my feet upon a rock," as is said in the thirty-ninth Psalm. What is the hole in the rock? If you see the sojourn of Jesus, conceiving the whole of him as a rock, you will see the hole in accordance with his sojourn, through which hole the things after God are contemplated. For such a thing is meant in the words "and you shall see my back parts."

But I have found one hole of one rock; I pass over in my discourse from the hole to the cleft of the rock, I seek also the many rocks. If I come to the chorus, whether of the prophets or of the apostles or even of the holy angels who have ascended higher, I say that all the imitators of Christ, since he is a rock, become rocks. And just as he has a hole through which the back parts of God are perceived, in the same manner each one, giving a way for God to be perceived through the things spoken by him, makes in himself a hole, or, if you wish to name it otherwise, a cleft. From which hole or cleft you will see, through Moses, the law, and through Isaiah his prophecy, and through Jeremiah other words of God. And if there is also an angel speaking, as he spoke according to what is said in the words "and the angel who speaks in me," there too I take my stand upon the angel, and I see there too a rock and a hole of a rock, and I see God angelically.

But I have need of an example, so that I may present how it is possible, having come to an angel, to see God also through the angel. For it is written in Exodus: "An angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in a flame of fire out of a bush. And Moses sees that the bush burns with fire, and the bush is not consumed." And the Scripture did not say, as it said at the beginning that "an angel appeared," so say that it was an angel of the Lord, but "I am the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob." God, then, was there being contemplated in the angel, as through the rock God is known, and through the hole that is in it.

You do not know, then, when the hunters are sent. On this account never come down from the mountains, nor leave the hills, nor be outside the clefts of the rocks; for if you are found outside, it will be said to you, as to one who happens to be outside and speaks the things of those outside: "Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be?" These things will be said to you; and these things too will be said to you, if you should say: "I will pull down my barns and build greater ones, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have good things laid up for many years; rest, eat, drink, be merry." You see the one below the mountains, the one below the hills, the one outside the clefts of the rocks, how he is deceived even in his judgment concerning good things, thinking these to be good things. Therefore he says: "And I will say to my soul: Soul, you have good things laid up for many years." He has reckoned the grain and the abundance of earthly things to be good things; for he did not see that the truly good things are not in the accursed earth, but the truly good things are in heaven. He was laying up treasure on earth, since he supposed that the things on earth were good. But if anyone should change from laying up treasure "on earth," being persuaded by Jesus, to laying up treasure "in heaven," it will not be said to him: "Fool, this night they demand your soul from you," but the hunters, coming, seeking not the things below but the living creatures in the mountains, those in the hills, those sheltered in the clefts of the rocks, will catch these and lead them away from that hunting. Where? To the rest of the holy and blessed ones in Christ Jesus.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
For "my eyes," he says, "are upon all their ways." Upon such as these, who make their haunts in the mountains and in the hills and in the clefts of the rocks, upon all their ways God has his eyes. "And they were not hidden from my face," such as these; for the wicked are hidden from the face of God. Adam, after the transgression, heard "the voice of the Lord God walking in the garden in the evening" and hid himself; but the holy one is not hidden, but has a heart with boldness before God in accordance with the holy conduct of life. For "if our conscience does not condemn us, we have boldness before God, and whatever we ask we receive from him." Now Adam, even if he sinned, did not sin a sin exceeding in grievousness; on this account he hid himself "from the face of God." But Cain, more sinful than he and most impious, the fratricide, what did he do? "He went out from the face of God." So that, by comparison of evils, to be hidden from the face of God is the lesser; for this one hides not shamelessly, but out of reverence for God. "They were not hidden," then, "from my face." These, who did these things, were once in sins and were fished up from the sins that are in the sea.

Therefore, that those who were fished up and afterward came to the mountains might not suppose that these things came about for them out of righteousness, the word reminds not only them but also us of our former sins. Therefore, after the benefits, it is said: "And their wrongdoings were not hidden from before my eyes."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
The following words are going to produce a struggle for us. For whether we understand them as consequent, we shall take careful thought concerning the recompense of sins; or whether they seem not to be consequent upon the things previously set forth concerning those fished up and hunted, in that way too they cast us into no ordinary struggle. For he says: "And I will first repay double their iniquities and their sins, whereby they profaned my land with the carcasses of their abominations and with their lawlessnesses, with which they filled my inheritance." Whether some, not understanding it, removed the word "first" from what was written, or whether the Seventy managed to remove it, God would know. We, however, comparing with the remaining editions, found it stands written: "And I will first repay double their iniquities," so that it may be made clear that, even if they should be worthy of blessedness on account of their later works, since they are human beings and have been in sins, they must first receive back their sins. And see whether the word is not true. Who will not receive back his sins except the one who, after believing and receiving forgiveness of sins (so as to hear Jesus saying: "Your sins are forgiven you"), no longer sins? But if after the forgiveness of sins and the dispensation of the washing of regeneration we should sin, as we, the many, who have not been perfected like the apostles, and after sinning and along with sinning we should also do some things duly, what awaits us must be considered. Then, if we depart from life having sins, but having also brave deeds, shall we be saved on account of the brave deeds, but released concerning the things sinned in knowledge? Or shall we be punished on account of the sins, but nowhere receive a reward for the brave deeds? But neither the one — I mean receiving back the worse things but not receiving the better — is in accordance with a just God, nor the other — I mean receiving back the better things but not receiving the worse — is in accordance with a just God, who wishes to purge and cut out wickedness. For suppose that you have built, upon the foundation Christ Jesus which you were taught, not only "gold and silver and precious stone" — if indeed you have gold, and much gold or little; suppose that you have silver, precious stone, and I say not these alone, but suppose that you have also "wood and hay and stubble" — what do you wish to happen to you after your departure? Whether at some point to enter into the holy places with your wood and with your hay and stubble, so that you may defile the kingdom of God? But again, do you wish to remain behind on account of the hay, on account of the wood, on account of the stubble in the fire, and to receive nothing for the gold and silver and precious stone? Neither is this reasonable.

What, then? First it follows that, on account of the wood, one receives back the fire that consumes the wood and the hay and the stubble; for our God is said in his essence, to those who are able to understand, to be a consuming fire. And the prophet was silent as to what it consumes when he said: "Our God is a consuming fire," but he left it to us to understand. When he said: "God is a consuming fire," there is something that is consumed. What, then, is that which is consumed? For he does not consume that which is according to his image and likeness, he does not consume his own creation, but the hay that was built upon, the wood that was built upon, the stubble that was built upon.

The passage was exceedingly hard to expound. There were promises, and after the promises he says: "And I will first repay double their iniquities." Of necessity the word "first" is added; for first the things of iniquity, then the things of righteousness are repaid, for God does not repay in reverse order. If he first repaid the good things, so that we might receive back the good things, but now he repays the evil things, the good things would have to cease, so that we might receive back the evil things. But first we shall receive back the evil things, and after these the good things, so that through the abolition of the evils the things of the chastisement of those who suffer may reach their end, so that after these he may repay the good things. Therefore you will find in the sacred Scriptures God speaking first the things that seem to be more gloomy and after these the better things. "I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal." "He himself makes to suffer pain and again restores; he struck, and his hands healed." Upon these things it is possible for the one who understands and is piously disposed toward what is said to say: "Lord, who shall sojourn in your tabernacle? Or who shall dwell in your holy mountain? He that walks blameless and works righteousness, that speaks truth in his heart; who did not deceive with his tongue, and did not do evil to his neighbor, and did not take up a reproach against those nearest to him." (But we reproach even those who repent and turn back, though the Scripture says: "Do not reproach a person who turns away from sin.") "He did not take up a reproach against those nearest to him; the evildoer is brought to nothing before him, but he glorifies those who fear the Lord." All of us, then, who have material for that fire, shall first receive back our sins.

But one of those who hear will say: expound also the word "double"; for suppose that I first receive back my sins, so that when I have received back the sins, after this there may be fulfilled what is said by the apostle: "If anyone's work shall be burned up, he shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved, yet so as through fire" — why then do I receive back my sins "double"? But it must be said that "the servant who knew the will of the master and did not act according to his will shall be beaten," not with few but with "many stripes." It is fitting, then, that those from among the nations who sin receive back their sins single, but that we receive back our faults double; "for if we sin willingly after receiving the knowledge of the truth, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sins, but a certain fearful expectation of judgment and a zeal of fire that is about to devour the adversaries." The things concerning those who would be fished up and hunted and would first receive back double their sins were prophesied. After these things the calling of the nations is prophesied more clearly, of those not being called but already called, and of those not not knowing what they should confess and for what they should give thanks, but of those who have already learned. For in the former things we were learning that they were called, fished up, hunted, but what they will experience in the latter things. Let us see what he prophesies concerning us who are already learning to pray, or rather have learned.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Lord, my strength and my help and my refuge in the day of evils; to you the nations shall come from the end of the earth and shall say: As false things did our fathers acquire idols, and there is no profit in them." From the end of the earth the nations came to God, and the nations have said: "As false things did our fathers acquire idols, and there is no profit in them"? How "from the end of the earth"? There are some who are first of the earth and there are some who are last of the earth. Who are the first? "The wise of the world" are first of the earth, not simply first; "the wise of the world, the well-born," the rich, the men of rank. Who are the last? "The foolish things of the world God has chosen, the base things, the things despised, the things that are not." "The nations shall come," then, "from the end of the earth," as if he said: from the last of the human beings on earth, from the foolish, from the base, from the despised, "and they shall say: As false things did our fathers acquire idols, and there is no profit in them." Not that there are some true idols, in contradistinction to which the false ones are spoken of, but idols which are by nature false; "and there is no profit in them."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "Shall a man make gods for himself?" Not only from images do human beings make gods for themselves, but you will find human beings making gods for themselves also from fabrications; for as many as are able to fabricate another god and another cosmogony besides the one recorded by the Spirit, a dispensation of the world besides the true world, all these have made gods for themselves and have worshiped the works of their hands. For instance, conceive for me, whether among the Greeks those who begot doctrines, say, of this philosophy or of that, or among the heresies those who first begot doctrines, these have made for themselves idols and fabrications of the soul, and turning aside have worshiped the works of their own hands, having accepted their own fabrications as truth. Convicting, then, all those who make gods for themselves both perceptibly and intelligibly, the word says: "Shall a man make gods for himself, and are these not gods? Therefore, behold, I will show them my hand at this time, and I will make known to them my power." At what time but this? And indicating the time of the coming of the Lord: "And they shall know," he says, "that my name is Lord."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then there is another prophecy, which — I do not know how — we did not find among the Seventy, but we found in the remaining editions, clearly lying in the Hebrew, and it is filled with matters most necessary, able, if we attend, to turn our soul back. And the words are thus: "The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, with an adamantine point engraved upon the breast of their heart." It is possible to give oneself over to the easier course and to say: these things are written concerning the Jews, that their sin "is written." But if you see, as we have often shown, Judah spoken of figuratively as Christ, perhaps "the sin of Judah" is ours who believe on Christ who is from the tribe of Judah. But if you are able to hear otherwise, in a more mystical way, perhaps he prophesies concerning Judas the betrayer, so that the prophecy is concerning him, saying: "The sin of Judas is written with a pen of iron, with an adamantine point engraved upon the breast of the heart"; but again the word "their" does not follow with respect to that man. Perhaps, then, he was speaking with reference to us, that, if we become sinners, these prophesied things overtake us. We have sinned, and our sin is not written outside us, but in our heart, and it is written "with a pen of iron, with an adamantine point." And that the sins which we sin are inscribed into us through the sinning, the matter itself will present. I was not conscious to myself of this or that matter or of this or that sin. Having done it, I have an imprint of it, and, as it were, there is written the imprint of my sin that has been sinned in my soul. And if my sin were written with ink, I would have wiped it out; but as it is, it is written "with a pen of iron," it is written "with an adamantine point," it is written "upon the breast of the heart" of ours, so that I may come to the tribunal and the prophecy be fulfilled that says: "There is nothing hidden that shall not be made manifest, and nothing covered that shall not be revealed." My breast was laid bare, and my heart having the letters of sin inscribed "with the pen," upon my breast and in my heart the imprints of my sins. "For there is nothing hidden that shall not be made manifest," but "amid one another the reasonings accusing or even defending," and "judge nothing before the time, until the Lord comes, who will both illuminate the hidden things of darkness and make manifest the counsels of the hearts." To whom will he make them manifest? Not to himself; for he himself knows "all things before their coming to be." But to whom, then, will he make them manifest? To all those who are going to see, on account of their own purity, the sin of the one who has sinned, so that the sinners "may rise up to reproach and to everlasting shame"; from which may the God of all deliver us, so that we may rise up to the glory that is in Christ, to whom is the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then, since many words have been gone through, there was indeed something to say about each of the things spoken, but time does not allow, as it presses upon us. Let us therefore speak on the passage read next: "Cursed is the man who has his hope on man." From this †, against those who suppose that the Son of God, the Savior, was but a man of God (for they dared, along with many of the evils of men, to say this also, that "the only-begotten," "the firstborn of all creation," is not God); for "cursed is he who has his hope on man." It is clear that they are cursed who have their hope on man. I would say that I do not have my hope on man, since, hoping on Christ Jesus, I do not know a man. Not only do I not know a man, but I know Wisdom, righteousness-itself, a man through whom "all things were created in the heavens and upon the earth, whether visible or invisible, whether principalities or authorities." "Cursed is the man who has his hope on man." Even if the Savior bears witness that the one he wore was a man—yet even if he was a man, still now he is by no means a man. For "even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, yet now we know him so no longer," says the apostle. I, through him, am no longer a man, if I follow his words; but he says, "I said, You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High." Therefore, just as he is "the firstborn from the dead," so he has become the firstborn of all men, having been transformed into God. "Cursed," then, "is the man who has his hope on man, and will make the flesh of his arm his support"—whoever ratifies the things of the flesh, whoever acquires bodily strength and wages war according to the flesh. But the holy man is not so; for "he does not make the flesh of his arm his support," since he "always" bears "the dying of Jesus in his body," and he mortifies "the members that are upon the earth, fornication, uncleanness." Having mortified these, he "does not make the flesh of his arm his support." "Cursed is he who has his hope on man." And at the same time this is against those who hope in dignities of rank. So-and-so is my friend, a centurion; he is a procurator; so-and-so is my friend and is rich and provides for me. Then to such a one also this is said: "Cursed is the man who has his hope on man." On no man do we hope, even if they seem to be our friends; for we hope not on them but on our Lord, who is Christ Jesus, to whom belong the glory and the might unto the ages of the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
On the notorious question we have come to see who the partridge is, concerning which Scripture now says: "The partridge cried out, it gathered what it did not bring forth, making its wealth not with judgment. In the midst of his days they shall forsake him, and at his end he shall be a fool." From the study of the nature of animals we must take up what has been recorded about the partridge, so that, knowing the facts about the animal, we may know whether the partridge now spoken of ought to be assigned to a better rank or to a worse one. It is said, then, to be a most malicious and crafty and cunning animal, one that wishes to deceive those who hunt it and that often rolls about the feet of the hunter, so as to draw him away, since the animal is nearby, in order that he may not come to the nest. And whenever it guesses that it has drawn the hunter off and that the chicks have fled, then it too flies away. And the animal is so utterly unclean that the males fight one another in single combat over mating, and male mounts male. If, then, this animal is both malicious and unclean, both cunning and deceitful, it is clear that to assign it to a better rank and to say that it can be referred to the Savior appears to be impious. We must therefore see, if we wish to interpret it of the adversary, whether the whole interpretation follows consistently for us.

The mother partridge cried out; she gathered what she did not bring forth. So then, the devil does not gather his own creatures; he does not gather what he begot, but whenever he cries out, he gathers the creatures of another and makes them his own. The partridge cried out through Valentinus, the partridge cried out through Marcion, it cried out through Basilides, through all the heterodox; for none of those men could utter the voice of Jesus: "My sheep will hear my voice." But the voice of Jesus is in Paul and Peter; wherefore Paul said, "If you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?" And the voice of the partridge, which gathered what it did not bring forth, is among those who lead astray and deceive the simpler among believers because of their innocence and their unpreparedness. "The partridge," therefore, "cried out, she gathered what she did not bring forth, making her wealth not with judgment." The partridge grew rich. See how many are her myriads: many have become the partridge's own, the myriads of the opposing power. And she made her wealth without taking thought for judgment, nor having any judgment, but acting without discrimination. Wherefore it is said that the partridge is "making her wealth not with judgment." But my Savior makes his wealth with judgment, and his wealth is judged and chosen out.

"In the midst" of "his days they will forsake him." We all who were once under the partridge that cried out — for it cried out not only through the things previously mentioned, but also through absolutely all who deceive and, as though summoning to piety, call people to godlessness, to doctrines contrary to the truth — but "in the midst of his days" we have forsaken him. For all his days are the days of this age; but since Christ Jesus has delivered "us out of the present evil age," for this reason "in the midst of his days" we have forsaken him. "And at his end he will be a fool." For when was he ever prudent, that at his end he should become a fool? But we will say that he was prudent; for "the serpent was the most prudent of all the beasts upon the earth which the Lord God had made." He was prudent according to what is said in Isaiah: "For I will bring punishment upon the great mind, the ruler of the Assyrians. For he said: By strength I will act, and by wisdom…"

…you may receive: "If anyone," he says, "seems to himself to be wise among you in this age, let him become a fool." He resolves it who earlier cried out: be foolish and stupid, that you may become wise. If, therefore, there is a certain blameworthy wisdom, according to which "the sons of this age are wiser than the sons of light in this generation," God is good, who overturns opposite things by their contraries, so that he may bring to fulfillment that which was said: "his last state will be foolish." When will his last state be foolish? Christ must "reign, until God puts all his enemies under his feet," and when he has subjected all things to him, "the last enemy, death, will be destroyed"; when death has been destroyed, then will come the last things of the partridge, and its last state will become foolish. So much concerning the partridge.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Now the beginning of the second chapter, which was read, is this: "A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is our place, our sanctification, our support, the support of Israel. O Lord, let all who have forsaken you be put to shame; departing, let them be written upon the earth, because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life." The blessed prophet Isaiah said, seeing the Lord and his kingdom: "I saw the Lord of Sabaoth sitting upon a throne lofty and lifted up." Jeremiah too saw how God reigns, on account of which, glorifying him, he says: "A throne of glory exalted from the beginning is our place, our sanctification." Whether you should wish to understand these words of Christ, you will not err, or of the Father, you will not think impiously: for the Savior is a lofty throne of glory and is from the beginning. "A throne of glory," because of which his kingdom is exalted; "our sanctification." [Our sanctification] is Christ; for "both he who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"The endurance of Israel." Just as the Savior is righteousness-itself, truth-itself, sanctification-itself, so also he is endurance-itself. And it is not possible either to be righteous apart from Christ, or holy apart from him, or to endure without having Christ. For he himself is the endurance of Israel. And even if you refer it to God, not even so will you be committing impiety.

"O Lord, let all who forsake you be put to shame, having departed from you." Each one of us, whenever he sins, through the things by which he sins forsakes Christ, and having forsaken Christ he forsakes God. For in doing wrong he forsakes righteousness, and in becoming profane he forsakes sanctification, and in making war he forsakes peace, and in coming to be under the enemy he forsakes redemption, and in being outside the wisdom of God he forsakes wisdom. To all, then, who forsake God the prophet utters an imprecation, teaching us what will befall them, saying, "Let all who forsake you be put to shame." As far as they have departed, let them be put to shame just so far. "Let them be written upon the earth." All human beings are written: the saints in heaven, but the sinners upon the earth. It is said to the disciples by Jesus, "Rejoice that your names are written in the heavens." Therefore one ought to rejoice, if he becomes such a person that his name is inscribed in the heavens. And just as the name of the saints is inscribed in the heavens, so the names of those who conduct their lives in an earthly manner — those who do not pass by the land of Edom but hold the fields of the land of Edom and the vineyards — are written, as of those who forsake God, upon the earth. For it says, "Let them be put to shame, having departed; let them be written upon the earth." For indeed, "with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you." Each is the cause to himself of his being written. So if you seek the things upon earth, you do not seek the things of heaven. If your soul has inclined toward the affairs of this place, you become the cause to yourself, since Jesus says, "Do not lay up for yourselves treasures upon the earth, where moth and rust destroy, and where thieves break through and steal; but lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven." Do you lay up treasure in heaven? You are the cause to yourself of your name being inscribed in the heavens. These things are on account of the phrase "Let them be written upon the earth." And he states the reason: "Because they have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life." And at the beginning the same prophet said, in the person of God, "They have forsaken me, the fountain of the water of life," and now, "They have forsaken the Lord, the fountain of life." Let us too, then, say — if indeed we wish not to forsake the Lord, the fountain of life — the utterance of the genuine disciples of Jesus, which they spoke to the teacher when he said to them, "Do you also wish to go away?" What, then, shall we say? "Lord, to whom shall we go away? You have the words of eternal life."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Then again there is a prayer that runs thus: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed; save me, and I shall be saved, for you are my boast. Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you, and I have not desired the day of man, you know it." To him alone who came for the sake of those who are sick, the physician who says, "Those who are strong have no need of a physician, but those who are sick," everyone who wishes to be cured of the sickness of his soul may confidently say, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." But if anyone else besides him professes the healing of souls, you would not be speaking truly if you said to that one, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed." For that woman too who "had a flow of blood" spent "all that she had" on the physicians, and "was not able to be healed by any of them"; for to none of those was it reasonable to say, "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed," but only to the one whom it suffices to touch "the fringe of his garment." I say therefore to this one: "Heal me, O Lord, and I shall be healed"; for if you heal, the end will follow upon the healing that comes from you, the cure, so that I may be saved. But however many others may save, I shall not be saved; but the only and true salvation is if Christ saves, since then I shall be saved. "A horse is false for salvation," and false too are all the other things apart from God for salvation. Therefore I would say to him: "Save me, O Lord, and I shall be saved." And I say this, if I am also able to say what follows by having renounced every boast, so that I may say, "For you are my boast," or when I fulfill the commandment that says, "Let not the wise man boast in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength, nor the rich man in his riches, but rather let him who boasts boast in this, to understand and to know that I am the Lord." Blessed therefore is he who has renounced all boasting here below, such as in what is called nobility of birth and in beauty and in bodily things, in wealth, in glory, and who is content with one boast, so that he may say, "For you are my boast."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Behold, they say to me, 'Where is the word of the Lord? Let it come.' But I have not grown weary in following after you." Jesus says to you, "Take up your cross, and follow me," and "Leave all things, and follow me," and "Whoever will not forsake his father and his mother and follow after me is not worthy to be my disciple." If, then, you become such a one as to follow Jesus always, you will indeed follow, and however far you follow you will not grow weary; for "there shall be no toil in Jacob, nor shall trouble be seen in Israel." There is no weariness for the one who follows Jesus; the very act of following takes away the weariness. For this reason he himself says—so that we may toil no longer, having toiled before we began to follow him—"Come to me, all you who toil and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest." If, then, though toiling we come to him and follow him, we shall say, "But I have not grown weary in following after you."

And to this it follows that we should also speak of the words "I have not desired the day of man." There is a certain day of man, and there is a certain day of God. Let each one of us desire the day of the resurrection of the saints, not that day of which it is written: "Woe to those who desire the day of the Lord; and this day is darkness and not light." Who is it that says, "And I have not desired the day of man"? The plain sense of the passage will convict us, that we have desired the day of man. Often, when we have fallen sick and have come to imagine death upon our departure, we entreat the brethren who watch over us and say: Ask for me a respite, ask that I may remain in this life. In saying these things we do not desire the holy day of God, but the day of man. Wherefore, having laid aside the love of life and the desiring of a human day, let us seek to see that day in which we shall attain the blessedness that is in Christ Jesus, to whom belong the glory and the might unto the ages. Amen.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
There are two visions of Jeremiah that have just been read, one following the other. The former of these contains what concerns the clay vessel in the potter's hand, which admits of restoration after being broken (for it is possible for it to be remolded); but the other vision contains what concerns the earthen jug, which, once shattered, admits of no cure. For when it was clay, if it was broken — even if it had already been given its shape — since it was clay, it was possible for it to become a second lump and to be fashioned a second time; but when, after being clay, it has already become earthenware and has been hardened by fire, then it was not possible, after the shattering of the earthenware, for any cure to come to it. What, then, these things intend, let us first consider by way of reflection, and then, if it be granted, let us examine them according to the letter. As long as we are in this life, we are being shaped — that I may so name it, on account of our clay vessel — in a potter's fashion, and we are shaped either according to vice or according to virtue. Yet we are shaped in such a way as to admit both that our vice may be shattered, so that a new and better creature may come to be, and that our progress may be dissolved after its shaping into a clay vessel. But when, after the present age, we arrive, having come to the end of life, and then, once fired — whether by the fire of the flaming darts of the evil one we become whatever we become, or by the divine fire (since indeed "our God is a consuming fire") — if, I say, we come to be under such or such a fire, whatever we become, if we are shattered, whether we were shattered and have perished from having become good vessels, or from having become wretched vessels, we are not created anew, nor does our structure admit of improvement. For this reason, as long as we are here, being as it were in the potter's hand, even if the vessel falls from his hands, it admits of cure and of being created anew. Let this much, then, be said somewhat more readily at hand, before we examine in argument what remains, concerning the two kinds of vessels: the clay one, not yet turned to potsherd, and the second, which has already become a potsherd.

But let us look, from the wording itself, at what is said about the clay vessel in the potter's hand, and how the very Word in the prophet, the Lord who prophesies in him, gives occasions — and others not slight — for the interpretation of the things concerning the molded thing in the potter's hand. "The word that came to Jeremiah from the Lord, saying: Arise and go down to the house of the potter." Jeremiah is above; he has ascended beyond the clay vessels. The clay vessels are below, and the nature that governs the clay vessels, condescending together with the things governed, is below. For this reason the word spoken to Jeremiah from the Lord says to him: "Arise and go down to the house of the potter, and there you shall hear my words." To Moses it is said, "Go up onto the mountain and hear"; to Jeremiah it is said, "Go down to the house of the potter and hear." For each of those who hear a word is either taught about the things above or learns about the things below. If I am taught the lower things, I descend by the word, that I may see the lower things; but if I learn the higher things, I ascend by the word to the higher things, that I may behold the things there.

But that all of you, so far as you are able, may follow along for yourselves with what is being said, I shall use an example, and one from Scripture, and in addition to the example I shall set forth a clarity that brings light to the interpretation that has been given. "In the name of Jesus every knee shall bow, of things heavenly and things earthly and things under the earth, and every tongue shall confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is unto the glory of God the Father." And there is a certain wisdom concerning each of these: a wisdom concerning the heavenly things, how the heavenly things are ordered; a wisdom concerning the things under the earth, since there is a wisdom of God also concerning the ordering of the things under the earth, and likewise concerning the earthly things. If I am going to have room for the wisdom concerning the heavenly things, I ascend to the heavenly things, as Moses ascended to the summit of the mountain, that the voice from heaven might become audible to him, according to what is written. For he was about to be taught heavenly forms of worship; for there was a shadow and a representation of heavenly mysteries in the laws of worship that have been recorded, as the apostle taught, saying: "who serve a representation and shadow of the heavenly things." As, then, when I am about to be taught concerning the heavenly things I ascend, so, if there be need for me to learn about the things under the earth, even should I become a prophet, I descend. And perhaps for this reason Samuel, when he was taught the things under the earth, went down below and came to be in Hades — not being judged so as to be in Hades, but that he might become a spy and a beholder of the mysteries of the things under the earth. Such too can be the things said by the apostle concerning wisdom, distinguished by the knowing of "what is the breadth and length and depth and height." You are going to know the height: you ascend by the word to the height; you are going to know the things between the height and the depth: you know the breadth and the length. Everywhere, guided by the word that teaches concerning all things, the mind that is able to follow the Son of God reaches. And it follows by renouncing the world and taking up the cross; for he is able to follow Jesus who is able to say: "to me the world has been crucified, and I to the world."

It was needful to explain the "Go down to the house of the potter, and there you shall hear my words." For it was needful to compare it with the "Go up and you shall hear my words." For of those who hear, some ascend that they may be taught — and they ascend not altogether bodily; while others descend and yet keep the soul above, in order to see the loftiest word concerning the lowest things. My Lord Jesus Christ himself both ascended and descended; "for he who ascended is himself also the one who descended above all the heavens." If, then, you too are going to understand the one who ascended most high as the word concerning the highest things, and the one who descended into the lowest things as him who teaches concerning the lowest things, "do not say: Who shall ascend into heaven? — that is, to bring Christ down; or, Who shall descend into the abyss? — that is, to bring Christ up from the dead. But what does the Scripture say? The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart," through which you ascend into heaven. And concerning the ascent, "the word is near you," and concerning the lowest things, "the word is near you"; for what else than the word that is everywhere can the holy one have within himself? For "the kingdom of heaven is within you."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The prophet, then, goes down to the house of the potter and recounts what he beheld, saying: "And behold, he was doing a work upon his hands, and the vessel which he was making of the clay fell apart in his hands; and again he made it into another vessel, as it pleased him to make it." But I do not know what the prophet saw when he came to the potter. For he saw the potter working; the vessel that had been made was of clay; the vessel fell apart. Why did he not say precisely: he let the vessel go out of his hand — nor did he lay the cause upon the potter? But since the word is about ensouled vessels, which fall apart of themselves, for this reason it is said: "the vessel fell apart from his hands." Take heed, then, to yourself as well, lest, while being in the potter's hand and still being molded, you fall apart from his hands by your own doing. For "no one snatches out of his hands," according to what is said in the Gospel according to John. Yet it is not written that, as no one snatches, so no one falls apart out of his hands; for free will is free. And I say: no one shall snatch out of the shepherd's hand, no one is able to take us out of God's hand; but we ourselves, by being negligent, are able to fall apart from his hands.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord." Each one understands the things written according to his ability, the one more superficially, as though drawing his understanding from them from a surface spring, the other more deeply, as one drawing up from a well. And both can be helped, since the same thing is for one a spring and for the other a well. The Gospel bears witness, when it recounts the things concerning the Samaritan woman; for there the same thing is named "spring" and "well," and in turn it is sometimes called a spring and sometimes a well. Let him who is able take note, that he may know that the same thing in its substance is for the superficial one a spring, but for the deeper one a well. This is for me a preface to the account that is coming, concerning the clay vessel that fell apart from the potter's hand and was again molded. Some have viewed these things more simply and have understood them. I shall set before you their account and interpretation; after this, if we have anything deeper, this too we shall recount. It is possible, they say, that here the things concerning the resurrection are indicated. For if the clay vessel fell apart from the potter's hands, and from the same material of the same clay he makes "it into another vessel as it pleased him before him," then the potter — God — of our bodies, the Craftsman of our structure, when this falls apart and is shattered for whatever cause, is able to take it up and renew it and make it a more beautiful and better "other vessel, as it pleased him before him to make."

Let this account too have its charm.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
But let us hear the Lord himself recounting and saying: "Shall I not be able to do to you as the potter, O house of Israel? says the Lord. Behold, as the clay of the potter, so are you in my hands. At the end I will speak against a nation and a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and that nation shall turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, and I will repent of the evils which I purposed to do to them. And at the end I will speak concerning a nation and a kingdom, to build it up and to plant it, and they shall do wicked things before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them, says the Lord." This concerning the house of the potter we see to be referred not to any of the individuals, but to two nations; for, beginning, he says that he is going to speak about nations, that he may suggest something to those able to hear hidden mysteries: "At the end I will speak against a nation." Seek both the end and the former nation, against which he speaks the things of destruction on account of their sins; and having spoken the things of destruction on account of the sins, he nonetheless promises that if they repent, he will repent concerning the evils which he said he would do to them. And again he speaks concerning another, a second nation, that a whole nation be "built up and planted"; and since this nation that is built up and planted has a good promise, but is able to sin, he says, after speaking these things, if they should depart from the good works: "I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them."

What, then, are the two nations — the one first named, to which the word threatens, and the second, to which it promises? Yet he threatens in such a way that, if it should repent, he does not carry out the things of the threat. He promises in such a way that, if the second nation should fall away and become unworthy of the promises, they should not obtain them. Concerning two nations especially is set forth the whole economy of God for the human beings in the world. That first nation, Israel, came to be first; second, from the sojourn of Christ, this present nation. To the former God threatened what he threatened, and we see the things of the threat against the former nation: it has come to be in captivity, their city was razed, the sanctuary was destroyed, the altar has been thrown down, nothing is any longer preserved of the things once held holy among them. For God said to that nation: Repent — and they did not repent. After these things were said to them, God speaks to this second nation the things concerning its being built up. But he sees that this nation too are human beings, able again to fall away. For this reason he threatens this one also and says: Even though I foretold the things concerning the building and the things concerning the planting and the husbandry, yet this nation too is going to sin, and to this one, having sinned, the same things will befall which were said to those others on account of the sins, and they will suffer them if they do not repent. Search the whole Scripture, and you will find most things spoken concerning these two nations. God chose the fathers, gave them a promise, led out a people from the race of the fathers out of Egypt, was long-suffering with them as they sinned, disciplined them as a father, brought them in, gave them a land of promise, sent them prophets at various times, disciplined them and turned them back from their sins. He was ever long-suffering, sending those who would heal, until the chief physician should come — the prophet surpassing prophets, the physician surpassing physicians. When he had come, they betrayed and killed him, saying, "Away, away with such a one from the earth; crucify, crucify him." Immediately a visitation came upon the nation; the place where my Jesus was crucified was made desolate; God chose another nation. See how great is the harvest, even if the laborers are few. And in another way too God orders that the dragnet always be cast upon the sea of this life, and fish of every kind are gathered; he sends "the many fishermen"; he sends "the many hunters," and they hunt from "every mountain," they hunt from "every hill." See how great is the economy concerning the salvation of the nations. "See, then, the kindness and severity of God: toward" the former nation, which also fell, "severity, but toward you," the second nation, promises and "kindness, if you continue in the kindness; since you too will be cut off." For the axe did not then lie against the root of the trees for that time only. The axe is ready to come again; and "the axe lies against the root of the trees," my Jesus was saying then, prophesying concerning Israel, against which the axe was. He himself was the axe of the unfruitful tree, and he said: "Already the axe lies against the root of the trees." As many trees as were there not producing fruit were cut down and cast into the fire and punished. But now another farmland has come to be, corresponding to the former, concerning which it is said: "Having brought them in, plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, in the prepared dwelling place of yours." God brought his nation into the mountain of his inheritance. The mountain I seek not as the Jews do, thus in inanimate materials. The mountain is Christ. In this we were planted, upon it we were kept. See, then, even if he be long-suffering, lest the master of the house, coming, should say: "For three years already I come to this fig tree and it has borne no fruit; cut it down; why does it even use up the ground?" For he uses up the good ground, Christ, the mystery of the Church, who comes to the assembly and does not bear fruit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"At the end I will speak against a nation or also against a kingdom." It will seem that "the end" is said simply. But it is said in this way. In the "I will speak against a nation or a kingdom," the "end" is of this sort: "I will raze" is said to the former nation as the "end"; to the second nation, "I will build you up." And again, "I will uproot" is said to the former ones, and "I will plant" to the second. Is it, then, that because the "end" has been spoken, the end must come to pass? God, though he does not repent, is said in Scripture to repent. And let us attend to the wording, that if we are able to give a defense of how these things are said, we may accept the account. "At the end I will speak," he says, "against a nation or against a kingdom, to remove them and to destroy them; and if that nation should turn from their evils of which I spoke against it, then I will repent concerning the evils which I purposed to do to them. And at the end I will speak concerning a nation or a kingdom, to be built up and to be planted, and they shall do wicked things before me, so as not to hear my voice, and I will repent concerning the good things which I said I would do to them." Concerning the repentance of God we are required to give a defense; for it seems to be a thing to be censured and unworthy — not only of God but even of the wise man — to repent. For I do not conceive of a wise man repenting; but the one who repents, so far as the customary use of the word goes, repents over not having deliberated well. But God, being foreknower of the things to come, cannot deliberate ill and, on account of this, repent. How, then, has the Scripture introduced him saying "I will repent" — not yet do I speak of what is said in the Books of Kingdoms in the "I repent that I anointed Saul as king," and what is said of him generally: "and repenting over the evils."

But see what we are taught concerning God generally. In one place, "God is not as a man, to be torn apart, nor as a son of man, to be threatened," and we learn through this wording that God is not as a man; but through another, which says that God is as a man: "that the Lord your God disciplined you, as if a man should discipline his son," and again, "he bore with the ways of his son as a man does." So then, when the Scriptures speak of God theologically in himself and do not interweave his economy with human affairs, they say that he is not as a man. For "of his greatness there shall be no end," and "he is fearful above all gods," and "praise him, all you angels of God; praise him, all his hosts; praise him, sun and moon; praise him, all you stars and light." And gathering countless other passages from the sacred writings you would find those to which you will fit the "God is not as a man." But when the divine economy is interwoven with human affairs, it bears the human mind and manner and expression. And just as we, if we converse with a two-year-old child, lisp on account of the child — for it is not possible for us, keeping the dignity of the mature man's age and speaking to children, without condescending to their speech, to understand the children — understand something of this sort for me concerning God also, when he orders the affairs of the human race, and especially of those who are still infants. See how we mature men also alter our words toward babies, and we name bread to them in a peculiar way, and we name the act of drinking by another expression, not using the mature speech which we use toward our grown-up peers, but some other childish and infantile expression. And if we name garments to the children, we assign to them other names, as it were fashioning a childish name. Are we, then, at that time imperfect? And if someone should hear us conversing with children, will he say that this old man has become foolish, that this man has forgotten his beard, the age of a man? Or is it granted, by way of accommodation, that one conversing with a child should not speak with the speech of an old man, nor with a complete one, but with a childish one?

And God indeed speaks to children; "behold," says the Savior also, "I and the children whom God has given me." It might be said to the old man who speaks to the child childishly — or, that I may say it more emphatically, infantilely — that you bore with the ways of your son and put on the manner of the infant and took up his condition. So, then, understand for me also the Scripture saying: "The Lord your God bore with your ways, as if a man should bear with the ways of his son." And it seems that those who translated from the Hebrew, not finding the word established among the Greeks, coined this one too, as in the case of many others, and made the "the Lord your God bore with your ways" (that is, he put on your ways), "as if a man should bear with the ways" (according to this example which I have given) "of his son." Since, therefore, we repent, when he converses with us who repent God says: I repent; and in threatening us he does not make a show of being a foreknower, but as speaking to infants he threatens. He does not make a show that he foreknew "all things before their coming to be," but as, that I may so name it, playing the part of the infant, he pretends not even to know the things to come. And so he threatens a nation on account of its sins and says: "If the nation repents, I too will repent." O God! When you threatened, did you not know whether the nation would repent or would not repent? And what? When you promised, did you not know whether the man — or the nation to which the word is addressed — would remain worthy of the promises, or would not remain? But he makes no show of it.

And many such human things you would find in the Scripture, as also the "Speak to the sons of Israel; perhaps they will hear and repent." This God did not say as one doubting, the "perhaps they will hear"; for God does not doubt, so as to say the "perhaps they will hear and repent," but that he may to a great degree make manifest your free will, and that you may not say: If he foreknew me as one perishing, I must perish; if he foreknew me as one to be saved, I must altogether be saved. He makes no show, then, of knowing about what is going to be concerning you, that he may preserve your free will by not having anticipated nor foreknown whether you will repent or not. And he says to the prophet: "Speak, perhaps they will repent." For countless other such things you will find said concerning God bearing with the ways of man. If you hear of the wrath of God and his anger, do not think the anger and the wrath to be passions of God. They are economies in the use of expressions, for the turning back and bettering of the infant; since we too make toward the children a face that is fearful not from disposition but by way of economy. If we keep the graciousness of the soul toward the infant in our face, and make manifest the tender affection which we have toward it, not distorting ourselves nor, as it were, changing toward its correction, we destroy it and make it worse. So, then, God also is said both to be angry and to be wrathful, that you may turn back and be bettered. And in truth he is neither angry nor wrathful; but you shall suffer the things of wrath and the things of anger, coming to be in pains hard to endure on account of your vice, when he disciplines you by what is called the wrath of God.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Next, after the discourse concerning the two nations — the former, to which the threat is given, and the second, to which the promise is given — he says (he said, that is, to the former ones): "And now I have spoken to the men of Judah and to those who dwell in Jerusalem; thus says the Lord: Behold, I am molding evils against you." Because these things which I am molding against you are in my hand, they can fall apart. Make these things fall apart from my hand, so that the evils which I am molding against you I may change and make into good things. You would not find, "Behold, I am molding good things against you," and the things said correspondingly after them, so that after this he might make manifest that the good things which he molds he releases from his hands, that he may make them evil. But he molds evils according to the example that has been mentioned, and, molding evils, he orders them wisely (apart from the interpretation that has been given for the "it fell from my hands"), so that, if it should fall, even the end of the evils being molded may come to be of a kind I do not know.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Let each one turn back, then, from his evil way, and make your practices better." Sometimes the more simple-minded say: blessed were the men of old, because they heard the Lord through the prophet saying, "and the Lord spoke to them." And to us now the Lord speaks through the things that are written: "Let each one turn back from his evil way"; the Lord himself converses with you, declaring, "and make your practices better." But those to whom the hortatory words concerning repentance were spoken made an answer, and let us see what they answered, so that we too may not answer in such a way. What, then, do they say in reply? "We will play the man, for we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart." And even if you do not say it in words, but your life is such that you sin, you too in effect say, through your evil deeds after the hortatory words, "We will play the man, for we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his evil heart." And what is "we will go after our own backslidings"? Those who have begun to put "their hand to the plow" and "who stretch forward to the things that are before" in their plowing, while "forgetting the things behind," have turned away from base things. Whenever, then, someone who has put "his hand to the plow" turns to the things behind, he will go "after his own backslidings"; for he will go after those things from which he turned away, and he runs back again to those sins which he had left behind. And so, of those who hear these things — whether catechumens who have left behind the gentile life, or believers who have already advanced in "stretching forward to the things that are before" — if the life has become depraved, they say nothing else than this very thing: "we will go after our own backslidings, and each of us will do the pleasing things of his heart" — not simply, but "of his evil heart, we will do." For there is an evil heart, and there is a good heart. Let no one, then, go "after his own backslidings," nor let him do "the pleasing things of his evil heart."

"Therefore," to those who answer thus, "the Lord says: Ask now among the nations: who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly?" And these things too will seem to have been said simply. But if the Church from among the nations turns to God in the manner it ought, it will be said: "Ask now among the nations: hear the dreadful things which the virgin Israel has done exceedingly." For let us compare the life of those who sinned with the life of those who turned back and believed, and we shall know that the former did dreadful things in killing "the Lord of glory," while the latter, when those had done dreadful things, turned to him who was taken away and put to death by them for the sins of the world. "Ask," then, "among the nations: who has heard such dreadful things as the virgin Israel has done exceedingly?"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
"Shall the breasts fail from the rock, or the snow from Lebanon? Or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind? For my people have forgotten me; they have burned incense in vain, and they shall grow weak in their ways, the everlasting paths, so as to walk in tracks that have no way for journeying, so as to make their land a desolation and a perpetual hissing." He has here spoken of differences of waters: first in "shall the breasts fail from the rock?"; second in "or the snow from Lebanon?"; third in "or shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind?" These three kinds of waters are the springs of the waters which the soul of the righteous, likened to the deer, longs for, so that each one may say: "As the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs for you, O God." Who, then, has become a deer, an enemy to the race of serpents, suffering nothing from their venom, as is recounted concerning the deer? Who has so thirsted for God as to say, "My soul thirsted for the living God"? Who has so thirsted for the breasts of the rock? "And the rock was Christ." Who has so thirsted for the Holy Spirit as to say, "As the deer longs for the springs of the waters, so my soul longs for you, O God"? If we do not thirst for the three springs of the waters, we shall find not even one spring of the waters. The Jews seemed to have thirsted for one spring of the waters, God; but since they did not thirst for Christ and the Holy Spirit, they cannot drink even from God. Those from the heresies seemed to have thirsted for Christ Jesus; but since they did not thirst for the Father, who is the God of the Law and the Prophets, therefore they do not drink even from Jesus Christ. And those who keep one God, but set at naught the prophecies and did not thirst for the Holy Spirit that is in the prophets, therefore do not drink even from the paternal spring, nor from him who cried out in the temple and said, "If anyone thirst, let him come to me and drink."

Therefore "the breasts from the rock" do not fail. But those men "forsook the spring of the water of life"; it was not the spring of the water of life that forsook them; for God removes himself far from no one, but "those who remove themselves far from him shall perish"; rather God draws near to some and meets the one who comes to him. When, at any rate, the son who had devoured the substance returned, the father met him. And he promises through the prophets, saying, "I will be nearer to them than the tunic to their skin." For "I am a God who draws near," he says, "and not a God from afar off, says the Lord." Therefore "the breasts shall not fail from the rock," the waters of Jesus, "nor the snow from Lebanon," the paternal waters. For frankincense (libanos) too is a sacred incense according to the Law of God, and it is offered upon the altar, "clear frankincense, equal part to equal part." And the mountain is called by the same name as this frankincense, and there is snow coming down from Lebanon, just as the water of the Holy Spirit, concerning which it is said, "Shall water be turned aside that is borne violently by the wind?" For indeed it is borne by the wind. The water of the Holy Spirit is not "turned aside," it does not flee, but each of us, by sinning, himself becomes a fugitive from drinking of the Holy Spirit.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "For my people have forgotten me, they have burned incense in vain." Everyone who sins has forgotten God, but the righteous one says, "All these things have come upon us, and we have not forgotten you, nor have we done wrong" — and he burned incense in vain. But what "they have burned incense in vain" means must be considered. If we take up again the things said earlier upon the hundred and fortieth Psalm, we shall understand what "they have burned incense in vain" is. Now there was in the Psalm something of this sort said: "Let my prayer be set forth as incense before you." Therefore my prayer, being composed of a fine heart — when our heart is not made gross — being sent up, becomes as incense before God. If, then, the prayer of the righteous is incense before God, the prayer of the unrighteous is indeed incense, but such incense that it may be said concerning it and concerning the unrighteous who prays, "they have burned incense in vain"; as is written concerning Judas, "Let his prayer become sin." That man, in his praying, burned incense in vain. And who it is that burns incense in vain, let us consider still further in this way. "Three times in the year," it says, "shall every male of yours appear before the Lord your God," to which is immediately added, "You shall not appear before me empty."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The apostle also knows vessels of wrath "made for destruction so that he might make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy." God has divided all people into these two vessels, those of wrath, those of mercy, those like Pharaoh and the Egyptians, those like Paul and those who have believed. But what is the treasury of the Lord in which are the vessels of wrath? Perhaps it is the church, in which such often go unnoticed. But there will be a time when he opens the church. For now they have been shut up, and the vessels of wrath share space with the vessels of mercy, and the chaff are with the wheat. In one net are the worthless and the chosen fish. The Lord opens up his treasury in the time of the judgment, when the vessels of wrath are thrown out.
